questions.questionHtml: Station A needs to send a message consisting of 15 packets to station ‘B’ using a sling window (window size 5) and go-back-N error control strategy. All packets are ready and immediately available for transmission. If every 6th packet that ‘A’ transmits gets lost (but no Acks from ‘B’ ever gets lost), then what is the number of packets that ‘A’ will transmit for sending the message to ‘B’ ?
questions.explanation: Message Size: 15 packets. Error Rate: Every 6th transmission fails. Window Size ($N$): 5. Receiver Window: 1 (discards everything out of order). Item Value Total Cycles 65 The total "time slots" used by the protocol (15 successful + 10 failed + 30 discarded + 10 empty). Total Packets Sent 55 The actual count of packets (1–15) put on the wire. Total Retransmissions 40 Wasted efforts: 10 lost packets + 30 packets discarded by the receiver. Empty Slots 10 Idle time at the end of the message when the window couldn't be filled. questions.questionText: Consider a file of size $4$ million bytes being transferred between two hosts connected via a path consisting of three consecutive links of bandwidth $2$ Mbps , $500$ kbps , and $1$ Mbps , respectively. All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file. Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file? Note: $1 \mathrm{M}=10^{6}, 1 \mathrm{k}=10^{3}$ $731$ $64$ $8$ $16$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a file of size $4$ million bytes being transferred between two hosts connected via a path consisting of three consecutive links of bandwidth $2$ Mbps , $500$ kbps , and $1$ Mbps , respectively. All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file.


Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file?

Note: $1 \mathrm{M}=10^{6}, 1 \mathrm{k}=10^{3}$

  1. $731$
  2. $64$
  3. $8$
  4. $16$
codeBlocks:
Bottleneck = min(2 Mbps, 500 kbps, 1 Mbps) = 500 kbps
File size = 4 × 10⁶ × 8 = 32 × 10⁶ bits
Time = 32 × 10⁶ / (500 × 10³) = 64 seconds

questions.questionHtml:
With respect to a TCP connection between a client and a server, which of the following statements is/are true? 

  1. The client and the server use a $2$-way handshake mechanism before the start of data transfer.
     
  2. A TCP connection is half-duplex. 
     
  3. The client and the server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time. 
     
  4. The server cannot initiate closing of the connection before the client initiates.

options.label: A
options.text: The client and the server use a $2$-way handshake mechanism before the start of data transfer.

options.label: C
options.text: The client and the server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time.

options.label: D
options.text: The server cannot initiate closing of the connection before the client initiates.

questions.explanation: Option-$\mathbf{A}$ The client and the server use a $2$-way handshake mechanism before the start of data transfer. Ans : False Reason : Before data transfer, TCP establishes the connection using a $3$-way handshake by exchanging SYN, SYN+ACK, and ACK segments. Option-$\mathbf{B}$ A TCP connection is half-duplex. Ans : False Reason : TCP offers full-duplex service. source: forouzan Option- $\mathbf{C}$ The client and the server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time. Ans : True Reason : Both the ends of TCP connection may send FIN segments at the same time. source: tanenbaum Option- $\mathbf{D}$ The sever cannot initiate closing of the connection before the client initiates. Ans : False Reason : TCP connection release can be initiated by either side (client or server). source: forouzan Answer : $\mathbf{(C)}$ benzene06 answered Feb 16 benzene06 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.title: CN - Data Link Layer
questions.explanation: Answer: (a) All four-bit errors occur only in parity bits. The two-dimensional parity scheme, with a global parity bit, can detect any odd number of errors and all 3-bit errors. It cannot detect all 4-bit errors, specifically those that form a rectangle in the data block (including parity bits). A 4-bit error pattern forming a rectangle (two errors in one row, two in another, same columns) will go undetected by both row and column parity checks, as parity for each affected row/column remains unchanged. However, if all four errors occur only within the parity bits themselves (row parity, column parity, or global parity), this specific configuration ensures that at least one row or column (or the global check) will detect an odd number of errors, guaranteeing detection. Other combinations (b, c, d) can form undetectable rectangular patterns involving data and parity bits.   https://gateoverflow.in/518110/cn-data-link-layer Het_Prajapati answered Jan 28 Het_Prajapati comment Share F

questions.questionText: Consider \(32\)-bit IPv4 addresses. The routing table is given below. \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{IP Prefix} & \text{Output Port} \\ \hline 00\ldots & \text{Port }4 \\ \hline 01\ldots & \text{Port }3 \\ \hline 010\ldots & \text{Port }5 \\ \hline 0111\ldots & \text{Port }9 \\ \hline 11\ldots & \text{Port }2 \\ \hline 00\ldots00 & \text{Port }8 \\ \hline \end{array} \] How many \(32\)-bit IPv4 addresses are forwarded along Port \(3\)? Reminder: \( 2^k - 2^{k-1} = 2^{k-1} \) \(2^{24}\) \(2^{26}\) \(2^{28}\) \(2^{30}\)
questions.questionHtml:
Consider \(32\)-bit IPv4 addresses.

The routing table is given below.

\[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{IP Prefix} & \text{Output Port} \\ \hline 00\ldots & \text{Port }4 \\ \hline 01\ldots & \text{Port }3 \\ \hline 010\ldots & \text{Port }5 \\ \hline 0111\ldots & \text{Port }9 \\ \hline 11\ldots & \text{Port }2 \\ \hline 00\ldots00 & \text{Port }8 \\ \hline \end{array} \]

How many \(32\)-bit IPv4 addresses are forwarded along Port \(3\)?

Reminder: \( 2^k - 2^{k-1} = 2^{k-1} \)

  1. \(2^{24}\)
     
  2. \(2^{26}\)
     
  3. \(2^{28}\)
     
  4. \(2^{30}\)
questions.explanation: Port $3$ corresponds to the $01..$ node. In this prefix, there are $30$ bits unset, so there are $2^{30} ~\mathrm{IPv}4$ addresses in this range. However, we have to subtract all the addresses in the $010$. range $(29$ bits unset, $2^{29}$ addresses$)$, and the $0111$ range $(28$ bits unset, $2^{28}$ addresses$)$, since they get forwarded out of different ports. This gives us a total of $2^{30}-2^{29}-2^{28}=2^{28}$ addresses forwarded along Port $3$. Another method is by realizing that only IPv4 addresses with $0110$ as its prefix will be forwarded along Port $3$, according to the trie. This means the next $28$ bits can each be either $0$ or $1$, totalling to $2^{28}$ possible addresses. Imagine a world having \(4\)-bit IP addresses.

Consider the routing table is given below.

\[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{IP Prefix} & \text{Output Port} \\ \hline 00\text{xx} & \text{Port }4 \\ \hline 01\text{xx} & \text{Port }3 \\ \hline 010\text{x} & \text{Port }5 \\ \hline 0111 & \text{Port }9 \\ \hline 11\text{xx} & \text{Port }2 \\ \hline 0000 & \text{Port }8 \\ \hline \end{array} \]

How many of the \(16\) possible \(4\)-bit IP addresses are forwarded along the default route?

Your answer should be a number between \(0\) and \(16\), inclusive.
questions.explanation: We have 4-bit IP addresses , so there are 16 total addresses : 0000 to 1111 . Routing uses longest-prefix match . Any address that matches at least one prefix in the table will not go to the default route. Only addresses that match none of the listed prefixes go to the default route. Routing table (interpreting x as “don’t care”): 00xx → matches 4 addresses: 0000–0011 01xx → matches 4 addresses: 0100–0111 010x → matches 2 addresses: 0100–0101 (but already covered by 01xx ) 0111 → matches 1 address: 0111 (already covered) 11xx → matches 4 addresses: 1100–1111 0000 → matches 1 address (already covered by 00xx ) Addresses covered by explicit routes 00xx : 4 01xx : 4 11xx : 4 Total covered = 12 addresses Default route Total addresses = 16 Covered addresses = 12 Uncovered addresses = 16 − 12 = 4 Those 4 uncovered addresses are the ones forwarded along the default route. learner_18 answered Jan 18 learner_18 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 10 10 vote

questions.questionText: A TCP packet has a value of \(9\) in its TCP header length field.  What is the size (in bytes) of the TCP options in this packet? \(9\) \(16\) \(20\) \(36\)
questions.questionHtml:
A TCP packet has a value of \(9\) in its TCP header length field. 

What is the size (in bytes) of the TCP options in this packet?

  1. \(9\)
  2. \(16\)
  3. \(20\)
  4. \(36\)
questions.explanation: Solution: The TCP header length field specifies the total TCP header size in units of \(4\) bytes. A value of \(9\) therefore corresponds to a total TCP header size of \[ 9 \times 4 = 36 \text{ bytes}. \] The minimum TCP header size (without options) is \(20\) bytes. Hence, the size of the TCP options is \[ 36 - 20 = 16 \text{ bytes}. \] Therefore, the correct answer is Option B .

questions.excerpt: Consider the network shown in the following diagram:Consider this simple network configuration between ETH and Swisscom. Assume that ETH owns a large IP prefix \(13.1.0.0...
questions.questionText: Consider the network shown in the following diagram: Consider this simple network configuration between ETH and Swisscom. Assume that ETH owns a large IP prefix \(13.1.0.0/17\), but only uses \(13.1.0.0/24\) to address its internal hosts. For simplicity, assume that ETH and Swisscom configure their forwarding tables statically and rely on the use of a default route \((0.0.0.0/0)\). Suppose Swisscom receives a packet for \(13.1.66.1\) from Deutsche Telekom. What is the path taken by this IP packet? Swisscom/1 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 → ETH/1 Swisscom/1 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 → Deutsche Telekom Swisscom/1 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 (packet is delivered to an ETH host) Swisscom/1 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 → …
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the network shown in the following diagram:

Consider this simple network configuration between ETH and Swisscom. Assume that ETH owns a large IP prefix \(13.1.0.0/17\), but only uses \(13.1.0.0/24\) to address its internal hosts. For simplicity, assume that ETH and Swisscom configure their forwarding tables statically and rely on the use of a default route \((0.0.0.0/0)\).

Suppose Swisscom receives a packet for \(13.1.66.1\) from Deutsche Telekom. What is the path taken by this IP packet?

  1. Swisscom/1 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 → ETH/1
     
  2. Swisscom/1 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 → Deutsche Telekom
     
  3. Swisscom/1 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 (packet is delivered to an ETH host)
     
  4. Swisscom/1 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 → …

options.label: C
options.text: Swisscom/1 → Swisscom/2 → ETH/0 (packet is delivered to an ETH host)

questions.explanation: Solution: The destination IP address is \(13.1.66.1\). This address belongs to the prefix \(13.1.0.0/17\), which is owned by ETH. Hence, when Swisscom receives the packet from Deutsche Telekom, it forwards the packet towards ETH according to its forwarding table. At ETH, only the prefix \(13.1.0.0/24\) is used to address internal hosts. The destination \(13.1.66.1\) does not belong to this prefix. Therefore, ETH does not find a more specific route and forwards the packet using its default route \((0.0.0.0/0)\), which points back to Swisscom. As a result, the packet is sent back to Swisscom, which again forwards it to ETH based on the prefix \(13.1.0.0/17\). This process repeats, leading to a forwarding loop. Thus, the path taken by the packet is: \[ \text{Swisscom/1} \rightarrow \text{Swisscom/2} \rightarrow \text{ETH/0} \rightarrow \text{Swisscom/2} \rightarrow \text{ETH/0} \rightarrow \cdots \] Hence, the correct answer is Option D .

questions.questionText: To transfer a web page of $9$ objects, non-persistent $\mathrm{HTTP}$ requires $18$ $\mathrm{RTTs}$ $(2~\mathrm{RTT}$ per object$)$. How many $\mathrm{RTTs}$ are needed for persistent $\mathrm{HTTP}$ without pipelining ?
questions.questionHtml:
To transfer a web page of $9$ objects, non-persistent $\mathrm{HTTP}$ requires $18$ $\mathrm{RTTs}$ $(2~\mathrm{RTT}$ per object$)$.

How many $\mathrm{RTTs}$ are needed for persistent $\mathrm{HTTP}$ without pipelining?
questions.explanation: Since the question says that for non-persistent HTTP, we require 2 RTTs per object, it implies that for every object, 1 RTT is used for TCP connection establishment and 1 RTT is used for object transfer. Hence, we should also count the TCP connection establishment RTT for persistent HTTP. For persistent HTTP (without pipelining), the RTT count is much smaller than that of non-persistent HTTP. 1 RTT to establish the TCP connection (3-way handshake). 1 RTT to request and receive the first object. After that, the same TCP connection is reused. Each of the remaining 8 objects needs 1 RTT each (request + response). Total RTTs: \[ 1 \;(\text{TCP setup}) + 1 \;(\text{first object}) + 8 \;(\text{remaining objects}) = 10 \text{ RTTs} \] If persistent HTTP with pipelining were used, all objects could be requested together, and the total RTT count would drop to 2 RTTs. However, unless explicitly mentioned, exams typically assume that pipelining is not used. Sachin Mittal 1 answered Jan 11 •

questions.questionText: Sender A transmits packets to intermediate node B using Go-Back-\(N\) with a window size of \(3\). Packets are indexed starting from \(0\). On the A–B link, packet $1 ~(\mathrm{pkt1})$ and packet $4 ~(\mathrm{pkt4})$ are lost during their first transmission. Node B forwards packets to receiver C using Selective Repeat with a window size of \(4\). When B finally receives $\mathrm{pkt4}$ from A and forwards it to C for the first time, $\mathrm{pkt4}$ arrives at C in error, so C does not acknowledge it. Which packets must B have sent to C after the first transmission of $\mathrm{pkt4}$ and before the timeout caused by $\mathrm{pkt4}$? A. None B. \( \{\text{pkt5}\} \) only C. \( \{\text{pkt5},\, \text{pkt6}\} \) D. \( \{\text{pkt6}\} \) only
questions.questionHtml:
Sender A transmits packets to intermediate node B using Go-Back-\(N\) with a window size of \(3\). Packets are indexed starting from \(0\). On the A–B link, packet $1 ~(\mathrm{pkt1})$ and packet $4 ~(\mathrm{pkt4})$ are lost during their first transmission.

Node B forwards packets to receiver C using Selective Repeat with a window size of \(4\). When B finally receives $\mathrm{pkt4}$ from A and forwards it to C for the first time, $\mathrm{pkt4}$ arrives at C in error, so C does not acknowledge it.

Which packets must B have sent to C after the first transmission of $\mathrm{pkt4}$ and before the timeout caused by $\mathrm{pkt4}$?

A. None
B. \( \{\text{pkt5}\} \) only
C. \( \{\text{pkt5},\, \text{pkt6}\} \)
D. \( \{\text{pkt6}\} \) only
questions.explanation: From the diagram, after the first transmission of pkt4 from B to C (which arrives in error at C), B continues to send the next packets inside its Selective Repeat window before the timeout for pkt4 occurs. Since pkt5 and pkt6 are transmitted before the timeout, the set of packets B must have sent to C after the first (failed) transmission of pkt4 and before the timeout is: \[ \{\text{pkt5},\ \text{pkt6}\}. \] Thus, B sends pkt5 and pkt6 to C before the timeout caused by pkt4. questions.questionText: A university campus is redesigning its legacy Ethernet network (Classic CSMA/CD) that operates at $1$ Gbps. The network engineers have specified that the maximum possible round-trip delay (including all repeater and queuing delays) between any two nodes in the network must not exceed $64$ bytes of transmission time for the protocol to work efficiently with the standard minimum frame size. What is the maximum permissible one-way propagation delay (in microseconds) for the network cabling to ensure that the $64$ -byte minimum frame size remains valid? Assume the speed of propagation in the cable is $2 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.
questions.questionHtml:
A university campus is redesigning its legacy Ethernet network (Classic CSMA/CD) that operates at $1$ Gbps. The network engineers have specified that the maximum possible round-trip delay (including all repeater and queuing delays) between any two nodes in the network must not exceed $64$ bytes of transmission time for the protocol to work efficiently with the standard minimum frame size.

What is the maximum permissible one-way propagation delay (in microseconds) for the network cabling to ensure that the $64$ -byte minimum frame size remains valid? Assume the speed of propagation in the cable is $2 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.
questions.explanation: Data rate $R=1 \mathrm{Gbps}=10^9 \mathrm{bps}$ Minimum frame size $L_{\text {min }}=64$ bytes $=512$ bits Propagation speed $v=2 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Requirement: Round-trip delay $\leq$ transmission time of 64-byte frame. Transmission time of 64-byte frame $$ T_{t x}=\frac{L_{\min }}{R}=\frac{512}{10^9}=0.512 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~s}=0.512 \mu \mathrm{~s} $$ This $T_{t x}$ is the maximum allowable round-trip delay. One-way propagation delay $$ T_{p r o p}^{o n e-w a y}=\frac{T_{t x}}{2}=\frac{0.512}{2} \mu \mathrm{~s}=0.256 \mu \mathrm{~s} $$ GO Classes answered Nov 28, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes 0.256 JAY_THAKAR answered Jan 9 JAY_THAKAR comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: A CSMA/CD protocol is surprisingly used on a geostationary satellite link between two ground stations. The data transmission rate on the link is $100$ Mbps . The distance between the two stations via the satellite is approximately $72,000 \mathrm{~km}$, and the speed of signal propagation is $3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. Calculate the minimum frame size (in bits) required for the CSMA/CD mechanism to function correctly on this link.
questions.questionHtml:
A CSMA/CD protocol is surprisingly used on a geostationary satellite link between two ground stations. The data transmission rate on the link is $100$ Mbps . The distance between the two stations via the satellite is approximately $72,000 \mathrm{~km}$, and the speed of signal propagation is $3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

Calculate the minimum frame size (in bits) required for the CSMA/CD mechanism to function correctly on this link.
questions.explanation: 48 Mbits Prince_Garg answered Jan 1 Prince_Garg comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Data rate $R=100 \mathrm{Mbps}=100 \times 10^6 \mathrm{bps}$ Distance $d=72,000 \mathrm{~km}=72 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~m}$ (round trip distance via satellite) Propagation speed $v=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Find round-trip propagation time $$ T_{p r o p}^{r o u n d}=\frac{2*d}{v}=\frac{2*72 \times 10^6}{3 \times 10^8}=0.48 \mathrm{~s} $$ For CSMA/CD, the frame transmission time must be at least the round-trip propagation delay: $$ \begin{gathered} T_{t x}^{\min } \geq T_{\text {prop }}^{\text {round }} \\ \frac{L_{\min }}{R} \geq 0.48 \mathrm{~s} \\ L_{\min } \geq 0.48 \times 100 \times 10^6 \\ L_{\min } \geq 48 \times 10^6 \mathrm{bits} \\ L_{\min }=48,000,000 \mathrm{bits} \end{gathered} $$ GO Classes answered Nov 28, 2025 • edited Nov 29, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a commen

questions.questionHtml:
A network contains $6$ routers P1 to P6 interconnected with the following link costs:

 

 

Routers exchange information using a distance vector algorithm.

Once routing stabilises, some links do not appear in the forwarding tables.

All such unused link costs are now changed to $1$, and the routing algorithm is executed again until stabilisation.

After reconvergence, how many links still remain unused?
questions.explanation: P1-P2: direct 4 vs via P1-P3-P2 $=6+2=8 \rightarrow$ use direct. P1-P3: direct $6 \rightarrow$ used. P2-P3: cost $2 \rightarrow$ used. P2-P4: direct 9 vs via P2-P3-P5-P4 $=2+8+2=12 \rightarrow$ direct 9 is used. P4-P5: cost $2 \rightarrow$ used. P5-P6: cost $3 \rightarrow$ used. P4-P6: direct 5 vs via P4-P5-P6 = $2+3=5$, equal DV will choose fewer hops → direct → so P4-P6 is used. → No Initial unused links Every edge is optimal. Hence no edge cost will be changed. Final answer: 0 GO Classes answered Nov 28, 2025 • edited Nov 28, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes 0 JAY_THAKAR answered Jan 9 JAY_THAKAR comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
Consider a network of $6$ routers, A1 to A6 with link costs as shown in the following diagram:

 

 

Assume a standard distance vector routing protocol is used.

Initially, some links are not chosen in the routing tables.

Now, all unused link costs are reduced to 3, and the algorithm is allowed to run again until convergence.

How many links remain unused after convergence?

  1. $0$
     
  2. $1$
     
  3. $2$
     
  4. $3$
questions.explanation: Shortest paths: A1 → A2: via $\mathrm{A} 1-\mathrm{A} 3-\mathrm{A} 2=4+3=7$ (better than direct 5 ? No → direct 5 is better.) So A1-A2 is used. $\mathrm{A} 1 \rightarrow \mathrm{~A} 3$ : direct $4 \rightarrow$ used. $\mathrm{A} 2 \rightarrow \mathrm{~A} 4$ : direct 6 vs via A3-A5-A4? A2-A3-A5-A4 = 3 + 10 + 1 = $14 \rightarrow$ worse So A2-A4 is used. A3 → A5: direct 10 vs via $\mathrm{A} 3-\mathrm{A} 2-\mathrm{A} 4-\mathrm{A} 5=3+6+1=10$ (equal) → both possible Typically DV chooses fewer-hop route → so direct A3-A5 is used. A4 → A6: A4-A5-A6 $=1+2=3$ (better than 7 ) → so edge A4-A6 is unused. Thus initially unused links are: A4-A6 Number of unused links $=1$ A4-A6: $7 \rightarrow 3$ Now recompute shortest paths: A4 → A6: direct $=3$ via A5 $=(1+2=3) \rightarrow$ equal → now direct is viable and will be used (DV usually prefers direct link). All links now lie on some shortest path. Final answer: 0 links remain unused GO Classes answered Nov 28, 2025 • edited Nov 29, 2025 by GO Cl

(Assume same propagation speed) $20 ~\text{meters}$ $50 ~\text{meters}$ $100 ~\text{meters}$ $10 ~\text{meters}$
questions.questionHtml:
A CSMA/CD network operates at $1 ~\text{Gbps}$ with a minimum frame size of $512 ~\text{bytes}$. The maximum segment length allowed is $200 ~\text{meters}$. If the data rate is increased to $10 ~\text{Gbps}$ while keeping the same minimum frame size, what is the new maximum segment length possible? (Assume same propagation speed)
 

  1. $20 ~\text{meters}$
     
  2. $50 ~\text{meters}$
     
  3. $100 ~\text{meters}$
     
  4. $10 ~\text{meters}$
questions.explanation: For CSMA/CD: $$ \frac{\text { Frame Size }}{\text { Data Rate }} \geq 2 \times \frac{\text { Segment Length }}{\text { Propagation Speed }} $$ Let: $F=$ frame size (bits) $R=$ data rate (bps) $L=$ segment length (m) $v=$ propagation speed (m/s) So: $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{F}{R} \geq 2 \times \frac{L}{v} \\\\ & L \leq \frac{F \times v}{2 \times R} \end{aligned} $$ $F=512 \text { bytes }=512 \times 8=4096 \text { bits }$ $R_1=1 \mathrm{Gbps}=10^9 \mathrm{bps}$ $L_1=200 \mathrm{~m}$ \begin{aligned} & \qquad 200=\frac{4096 \times v}{2 \times 10^9} \\\\ & 200 \times 2 \times 10^9=4096 \times v \\\\ & 4 \times 10^{11}=4096 \times v \\\\ & v=\frac{4 \times 10^{11}}{4096} \\\\ & v=\frac{4 \times 10^{11}}{4.096 \times 10^3} \\\\ & v \approx 9.765625 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned} $F \text { same }=4096 \text { bits }$ $R_2=10 \mathrm{Gbps}=10^{10} \mathrm{bps}$ $v \text { same }=9.765625 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ \begin{aligned

questions.questionHtml:
An IP datagram of $4000 ~\text{bytes}$ (including $20$-$\text{byte}$ IP header) passes through a network with $\text{MTU} = 1500 ~\text{bytes}$
How many fragments are created, and what is the total size (sum of all fragments including headers) after fragmentation?
 

  1. $3 ~\text{fragments}, 4020 ~\text{bytes}$
     
  2. $3 ~\text{fragments}, 4040 ~\text{bytes}$
     
  3. $4 ~\text{fragments}, 4040 ~\text{bytes}$
     
  4. $4 ~\text{fragments}, 4060 ~\text{bytes}$
questions.explanation: Given: Original datagram size: \[ 4000 \text{ bytes (including 20-byte IP header)} \] Payload size: \[ 4000 - 20 = 3980 \text{ bytes} \] MTU constraint: \[ 1500 \text{ bytes} \Rightarrow \text{(header + data)} \le 1500 \text{ bytes} \] Each fragment gets a fresh 20-byte IP Header Fragment offset requirement: Non-last fragment data size must be a multiple of 8 bytes Maximum data per fragment: \[ 1500 - 20 = 1480 \text{ bytes} \] Check alignment: \[ \frac{1480}{8} = 185 \quad \text{(integer → valid)} \] So each of the first fragments will carry 1480 bytes of data. Fragmentation: Fragment 1 data = 1480 bytes   Fragment 2 data = 1480 bytes   Used so far: \[ 1480 + 1480 = 2960 \text{ bytes} \] Remaining: \[ 3980 - 2960 = 1020 \text{ bytes} \] So third fragment data = 1020 bytes. Fragment sizes including headers: \[ \text{Fragment 1} = 1480 + 20 = 1500 \text{ bytes} \] \[ \text{Fragment 2} = 1480 + 20 = 1500 \text{ bytes} \] \[ \text{Fragment 3} = 1020 + 20 = 1040 \text{ bytes} \]

Consider a TCP connection using AIMD (Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease) congestion control. The current congestion window size is $\mathbf{2 4 ~MSS}$. A timeout occurs, followed by three successful RTTs of transmission.

What is the congestion window size after these three RTTs?
questions.explanation: After Timeout When a timeout occurs, TCP enters slow start phase: Congestion window (cwnd) is set to $1 ~\mathrm{MSS}$ Slow start threshold (ssthresh) is set to half of previous window: $24 / 2=12 ~\mathrm{MSS}$ First RTT (Slow Start) $\mathrm{cwnd = 1 ~MSS \rightarrow 2 ~MSS}$ (exponential increase in slow start) Second RTT (Slow Start continues) $\mathrm{cwnd =2 ~MSS \rightarrow 4 ~MSS}$ (exponential increase) Still below ssthresh $\mathrm{(12 ~MSS)}$, so slow start continues. Third RTT (Still in Slow Start) $\mathrm{cwnd =4 ~MSS \rightarrow 8 ~MSS}$ (exponential increase) Now $\text{cwnd} ~(8 ~\mathrm{MSS})$ is still less than $\text{ssthresh}~(12 ~\mathrm{MSS})$ Final Window Size After three successful RTTs, the congestion window size is $\mathbf{8 ~MSS}$. The IP header size is $\mathbf{20 ~bytes}$. The datagram needs to be fragmented to traverse this network. What is the total overhead (in $\textbf{bytes}$) introduced due to fragmentation? $\mathrm{40 ~bytes}$ $\mathrm{60 ~bytes}$ $\mathrm{80 ~bytes}$ $\mathrm{100 ~bytes}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider an IP datagram of $\mathbf{1500 ~bytes}$ (including the IP header) that must be sent over a network with an MTU of $\mathbf{576 ~bytes}$. The IP header size is $\mathbf{20 ~bytes}$.

The datagram needs to be fragmented to traverse this network.

What is the total overhead (in $\textbf{bytes}$) introduced due to fragmentation?
 

  1. $\mathrm{40 ~bytes}$
     
  2. $\mathrm{60 ~bytes}$
     
  3. $\mathrm{80 ~bytes}$
     
  4. $\mathrm{100 ~bytes}$
questions.explanation: Total size = $1500 ~\text{bytes}$ IP header = $20 ~\text{bytes}$ Data payload $=1500-20=1480 ~\text{bytes}$ MTU = $576 ~\text{bytes}$ Each fragment needs a $20 ~\text{byte}$ IP header Maximum data per fragment $=$ MTU - IP header $=576-20=556 ~\text{bytes}$ Total data to fragment = $1480 ~\text{bytes}$ Data per fragment = $556 ~\text{bytes}$ Number of fragments $=\lceil 1480 / 556\rceil=\lceil 2.662\rceil=3 ~\text{fragments}$ Fragment 1 data = $556 ~\text{bytes}$ Fragment 2 data $=556 ~\text{bytes}$ Fragment 3 data $=1480-(556 \times 2)=368 ~\text{bytes}$ Original datagram: 1 header $=20 ~\text{bytes}$ After fragmentation: 3 headers $=3 \times 20=60 ~\text{bytes}$ Overhead $=$ Total headers after - Total headers before $=60-20=\mathbf{40 ~bytes}$ Final Answer: (A)  $\mathbf{40 ~bytes}$ GO Classes answered Nov 21, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes A JAY_THAKAR answered Jan 11 JAY_THAKAR comment Share Follow 0 re

questions.questionHtml:
A company has been assigned the IP block $\verb|192.168.10.0/24|$.

The network administrator wants to create $\mathbf{6 ~subnets}$, each capable of accommodating at least $\mathbf{25}$ usable host addresses.

Which of the following subnet masks should be used, and what will be the total number of usable subnets and usable hosts per subnet created?

 

  1. $/ 26 \rightarrow 4$ subnets, $62$ hosts per subnet
     
  2. $/ 27 \rightarrow 8$ subnets, $30$ hosts per subnet
     
  3. $/ 28 \rightarrow 16$ subnets, $14$ hosts per subnet
     
  4. $/ 29 \rightarrow 32$ subnets, $6$ hosts per subnet
questions.explanation: Subnet size for $/ 27=2^{\wedge}(32-27)=2^{\wedge} 5=32$ addresses. Usable hosts per subnet $=32-2=30$. Number of subnets from $/ 24 \rightarrow / 27=2^{\wedge}(27-24)=2^{\wedge} 3=8$. $8$ subnets $\geq 6$ required and 30 hosts $\geq 25$ required, so $/ 27$ satisfies both conditions. questions.questionHtml:
A leaky bucket algorithm is configured to leak at a constant rate of $\mathbf{1,000}$ bytes per second. The bucket capacity is $\mathbf{5,000}$ bytes.

Packets of $\mathbf{2,000}$ bytes arrive at $\mathbf{t = 0 ~s, ~t=1 ~s, ~t=2 ~s, ~t=3 ~s,}$ and $\mathbf{t=4~s}$.

Assume the bucket starts empty and no packet loss occurs.
 

At what earliest time will the last packet completely leave the bucket?
 

  1. $8 ~\mathrm{seconds}$
     
  2. $9 ~\mathrm{seconds}$
     
  3. $10 ~\mathrm{seconds}$
     
  4. $11 ~\mathrm{seconds}$
questions.explanation: Leak rate $=1,000$ bytes $/ \mathrm{s}$. Packet arrivals (each $2,000$ bytes) at $\mathrm{t}=0,1,2,3,4 \mathrm{~s}$. (Bucket starts empty.) Timeline (level = bytes in bucket): $\mathrm{t}=0$ after arrival = $2000$ $\mathrm{t}=1$ before arrival $=2000-1000=1000$; after arrival $=1000+2000=3000$ $\mathrm{t}=2$ before arrival $=3000-1000=2000$; after arrival $=2000+2000=4000$ $\mathrm{t}=3$ before arrival $=4000-1000=3000$; after arrival $=3000+2000=5000$ $\mathrm{t}=4$ before arrival $=5000-1000=4000$; after arrival $=4000+2000=6000$ (After the last arrival at $\mathrm{t}=4 \mathrm{~s}$ the bucket contains $6000$ bytes.) Time to drain $6000$ bytes at 1000 bytes $/ \mathrm{s}=6000 \div 1000=6 \mathrm{~s}$. Finish time $=4+6=10$ seconds. Note: the stated bucket capacity ($5,000$ bytes) would be exceeded at $\mathrm{t}=4$ (would reach $6,000$). Since the problem explicitly instructs to assume no packet loss, we proceed ignoring overflow; with no-loss assumption the completion time is $10\m

questions.questionHtml:
A network link uses a token bucket for traffic shaping with a bucket size of $\mathbf{10,000}$ tokens and a token generation rate of $\mathbf{2000}$ tokens per second. Each token allows transmission of $\mathbf{1}$ byte.

A source wants to send $\mathbf{20,000}$ bytes of data as fast as possible through this link.
Assume the output link can transmit at a very high rate, and tokens are consumed only when packets are sent.

Find the minimum time required to send all $20,000$ bytes.
 

  1. $3 ~\textrm{seconds}$
     
  2. $4 ~\textrm{seconds}$
     
  3. $5 ~\textrm{seconds}$
     
  4. $6 ~\textrm{seconds}$
questions.explanation: Initial tokens in bucket = $10,000$. Data to send = $20,000$ bytes. You can send $10,000$ bytes immediately using existing tokens, leaving $10,000$ bytes to be covered by newly generated tokens. Token generation rate $=2,000$ tokens $/ \mathrm{sec} \rightarrow$ time to generate remaining $10,000$ tokens $=10,000 \div 2,000=5$ seconds. Minimum time to send all 20,000 bytes $=5$ seconds. Answer: C ($5 ~\mathrm{seconds}$) GO Classes answered Nov 19, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. A leaky bucket algorithm is used for traffic shaping. The bucket leaks at a constant rate of $\mathbf{10 ~KB/s}$ and has a capacity of $\mathbf{3 0 ~ K B}$ .

Assuming no other data arrives later, how long will it take for the bucket to empty completely?

  2. $3$ $\mathrm{seconds}$
     
  3. $4$ $\mathrm{seconds}$
     
  4. $5$ $\mathrm{seconds}$
questions.explanation: Leak rate $=10 \mathrm{~KB/s}$ Bucket capacity $=30 \mathrm{~KB}$ Incoming burst $=50 \mathrm{~KB}$ (arrives instantaneously) Out of $50 \mathrm{~KB}$ , only $30 \mathrm{~KB}$ fits into the bucket. Remaining $30 \mathrm{~KB}$ is discarded (overflow). The bucket leaks at a fixed rate of $10 \mathrm{~KB/s}$. So, time to empty $30 \mathrm{~KB}=30 \div 10=\mathbf{3~seconds}$. questions.questionHtml:
Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of $1400 \textbf{ bytes}$ in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is $6800 \textbf{ bytes}$.

Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including the IPv4 header?
 

  1. $4 \mathrm{~fragments} ~1400 \mathrm{~bytes}$
     
  2. $5 \mathrm{~fragments} ~1316 \mathrm{~bytes}$
     
  3. $6 \mathrm{~fragments} ~108 \mathrm{~bytes}$
     
  4. $5 \mathrm{~fragments} ~1296 \mathrm{~bytes}$
questions.explanation: UDP Payload = 6800 bytes So total size of UDP User Datagram = 6800 + UDP header = 6808 bytes Ethernet frame max payload = 1400 byes So IP max payload = 1400 - 20 (header of IP) = 1380 bytes But 1380 is not divisible by 8, we want fragment size to be divisible by 8. So fragment size will be nearest lower no divisible by 8, which is 1376. Total fragments = ceiling(6808/1376) = 5 So 5 total fragments Last fragment UDP User Datagram size = 6808 - 4*1376 = 1304 Last fragment frame payload size = UDP size + IP header size = 1304 + 20 = 1324 bytes So answer is 5 fragments, 1324 byes As of the current options, no answer matches mv_ind answered Nov 20, 2025 1 flag: ✌ Edit necessary (js__ “1316 B”) mv_ind comment Share Follow See all 3 Comments 3 3 Comments reply Prince_Garg commented Dec 20, 2025 reply Follow flag Option B is Correct There were 4 fragments of total size(including header) 1396 and the 5th fragment will be of total size 1316.

CONSIDER A COMPUTER C1 CONFIGURED AS FOLLOWS:

  • IP ADDRESS: $\texttt{192.168.10.100}$
     
  • SUBNET MASK: $\texttt{255.255.255.192}$
     
  • DEFAULT GATEWAY: $\texttt{192.168.10.65}$
     

C1 WANTS TO SEND A PACKET TO A SECOND COMPUTER, C2, WHICH HAS THE IP ADDRESS $\texttt{192.168.10.200}$.

WHICH IP ADDRESS WILL C1 SEND AN ARP REQUEST FOR?
 

  1. $\texttt{192.168.10.200}$
     
  2. $\texttt{192.168.10.65}$
     
  3. $\texttt{192.168.10.64}$
     
  4. $\texttt{192.168.10.127}$
questions.explanation: Determine C1's Subnet: C1 must first determine if the destination IP ( $\texttt{192.168.10.200}$ ) is on its own local subnet. It does this by comparing its own network ID to the destination's network ID, using its own subnet mask. C1's Subnet Mask: $\texttt{255.255.255.192}$ C1's Network ID ( $\texttt{192.168.10.64}$ ) is different from C2's Network ID ( $\texttt{192.168.10.192}$ ). This means C2 is on a remote network. To send a packet to a remote network, C1 must send the packet to its Default Gateway. C1 will send an ARP request to find the MAC address of its Default Gateway, which is $\texttt{192.168.10.65}$. questions.questionText: A SENDER USES THE SELECTIVE REPEAT SLIDING WINDOW PROTOCOL AND USES $\mathbf{7}$  BITS FOR THE SEQUENCE NUMBER. DATA PACKETS ARE $\mathbf{1}$ KB ($1000$ BYTES) IN SIZE. THE ONE-WAY PROPAGATION DELAY IS $\mathbf{2 5}$  msec. ASSUME $W_S=W_R$ AND THE TOTAL SEQUENCE SPACE IS FULLY UTILIZED. WHAT IS THE MINIMUM LINK BANDWIDTH (IN Mbps) REQUIRED TO ACHIEVE A LINK UTILIZATION OF EXACTLY $\mathbf{8 0 \%}$ ? $10.1$ Mbps $12.6$ Mbps $14.2$ Mbps $20.5$ Mbps
questions.questionHtml:
A SENDER USES THE SELECTIVE REPEAT SLIDING WINDOW PROTOCOL AND USES $\mathbf{7}$ BITS FOR THE SEQUENCE NUMBER.

  • DATA PACKETS ARE $\mathbf{1}$ KB ($1000$ BYTES) IN SIZE.
     
  • THE ONE-WAY PROPAGATION DELAY IS $\mathbf{2 5}$ msec.
     
  • ASSUME $W_S=W_R$ AND THE TOTAL SEQUENCE SPACE IS FULLY UTILIZED.
     

WHAT IS THE MINIMUM LINK BANDWIDTH (IN Mbps) REQUIRED TO ACHIEVE A LINK UTILIZATION OF EXACTLY $\mathbf{8 0 \%}$ ?
 

  1. $10.1$ Mbps
     
  2. $12.6$ Mbps
     
  3. $14.2$ Mbps
     
  4. $20.5$ Mbps
questions.explanation: Protocol is Selective Repeat. Sequence bits $(k)=7$. Total sequence space $=2^k=2^7=128$. The rule for SR is $W_S+W_R \leq 2^k$. Given $W_S=W_R$ and the space is fully utilized, $W_S+W_S=128$. $$2 \times W_S=128 \Longrightarrow W_S=\mathbf{6 4}$$ $$W=64 .$$ $\eta$ (Utilization) $=80 \%=0.8$ $L$ (Frame Size) $=1000$ Bytes $=8,000$ bits $T_p$ (One-way) $=25 \mathrm{msec}=0.025$ seconds RTT $=2 \times T_p=0.050$ seconds $$ T_t=L / B=8,000 / B $$ \begin{aligned} & \eta=\left(W \times T_t\right) /\left(T_t+R T T\right) \\\\ & 0.8=(64 \times(8000 / B)) /((8000 / B)+0.05) \\\\ & 0.8 \times((8000 / B)+0.05)=64 \times(8000 / B) \\\\ & (0.8 \times 8000 / B)+(0.8 \times 0.05)=512,000 / B \\\\ & (6400 / B)+0.04=512,000 / B \\\\ & 0.04=(512,000 / B)-(6400 / B) \\\\ & 0.04=(512,000-6400) / B \\\\ & 0.04=505,600 / B \\\\ & B=505,600 / 0.04 \\\\ & B=12,640,000 \text { bits/second } \\\\ & B=12,640,000 / 10^6 \mathrm{Mbps}=\mathbf{1 2 . 6 4} \mathrm{Mbps} \e

questions.questionText: A TCP connection uses $\mathbf{32-}$ bit sequence numbers , which means there are $2^{32}$ (about $4.3$ billion) unique byte-counts. A network has a Maximum Packet Lifetime (MPL) of $\mathbf{100}$  seconds . This is a guarantee that no packet will stay "lost" in the network for more than $100$ seconds. To prevent errors, the connection's data rate must be slow enough that it cannot "wrap around" (use all $2^{32}$ sequence numbers) in less than $100$ seconds. What is the maximum data rate (in Bytes per second) that this connection can safely support? $2^{32} \mathrm{~B} / \mathrm{S}$ $100 \mathrm{~B} / \mathrm{S}$ $2^{32} \div 100 \mathrm{~B} / \mathrm{S}$ $100 \div 2^{32} \mathrm{~B} / \mathrm{S}$
questions.questionHtml:
A TCP connection uses $\mathbf{32-}$bit sequence numbers, which means there are $2^{32}$ (about $4.3$ billion) unique byte-counts.

A network has a Maximum Packet Lifetime (MPL) of $\mathbf{100}$ seconds. This is a guarantee that no packet will stay "lost" in the network for more than $100$ seconds.

To prevent errors, the connection's data rate must be slow enough that it cannot "wrap around" (use all $2^{32}$ sequence numbers) in less than $100$ seconds.

What is the maximum data rate (in Bytes per second) that this connection can safely support?

  1. $2^{32} \mathrm{~B} / \mathrm{S}$
     
  2. $100 \mathrm{~B} / \mathrm{S}$
     
  3. $2^{32} \div 100 \mathrm{~B} / \mathrm{S}$
     
  4. $100 \div 2^{32} \mathrm{~B} / \mathrm{S}$
questions.explanation: Identify the Goal: We need to find the maximum safe data rate. Identify the Constraint: The time it takes to use all sequence numbers ( $T_{\text {wrap }}$ ) must be greater than the Maximum Packet Lifetime (MPL). $T_{\text {wrap }}>\mathrm{MPL}$ Define the Variables: Sequence Space ( $S$ ): $2^{32}$ Bytes MPL: 100 seconds Rate ( $R$ ): The data rate in Bytes/second. Find the Wrap Time: The time to wrap is the total amount of data (the sequence space) divided by the data rate. $T_{\text {wrap }}=$ Sequence Space $/$ Rate $=S / R$ Set up the Inequality: We substitute our equation from step 4 into the constraint from step 2. $(S / R)>\mathrm{MPL}$ Solve for the Rate $(R)$ : We need to find the maximum $R$. Let's rearrange the inequality: $S>\mathrm{MPL} \times R$ $S / \mathrm{MPL}>R$ This means the Rate ( $R$ ) must be less than $S / \mathrm{MPL}$. questions.questionHtml:
A SENDER USES THE STOP-AND-WAIT ARQ PROTOCOL.

  • THE SIZE OF A DATA FRAME IS $\mathbf{2000}$ BYTES.
     
  • THE SIZE OF AN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT IS $\mathbf{50}$ BYTES.
     
  • THE ONE-WAY PROPAGATION DELAY IS $\mathbf{1 5 0}$ MILLISECONDS.
     
  • THE RECEIVER'S TRANSMISSION RATE IS $1/10$TH OF THE SENDER'S TRANSMISSION RATE.
     
  • ASSUME NO FRAME IS LOST AND PROCESSING DELAYS ARE NEGLIGIBLE.
     

TO ACHIEVE A SENDER THROUGHPUT OF EXACTLY $5000$ BYTES/SECOND, THE SENDER'S TRANSMISSION RATE MUST BE $\_\_\_\_$ KBPS ( $1$ KBPS $=1000$ BITS/SECOND).
questions.explanation: Given Throughput: $5000 \mathrm{~B} / \mathrm{s}$ Data Frame Size ( $L_D$ ): $2000$ Bytes ACK Frame Size ( $L_A$ ): $50$ Bytes One-way $T_p: 150 \mathrm{~ms}=0.15 \mathrm{~seconds}$ Round-trip Propagation Delay $\left(2 \times T_p\right)$ : $0.3$ seconds Sender Bandwidth: $B$ (in $\mathrm{B} / \mathrm{s}$ ) Receiver Bandwidth: $B / 10$ (in $\mathrm{B} / \mathrm{s}$ ) The total time for one cycle (sending one frame and receiving its ACK) is: $$ R T T=T_{t x D}+T_{t x A}+\left(2 \times T_p\right) $$ Data Tx Time $\left(T_{t x D}\right): \frac{L_D}{B}=\frac{2000}{B}$ seconds ACK Tx Time $\left(T_{t x A}\right): \frac{L_A}{B / 10}=\frac{50}{B / 10}=\frac{500}{B}$ seconds Propagation Delay: 0.3 seconds $$ R T T=\frac{2000}{B}+\frac{500}{B}+0.3=\frac{2500}{B}+0.3 $$ Throughput is the useful data sent divided by the total cycle time: $$ \text { Throughput }=\frac{L_D}{R T T} $$ \begin{aligned} & 5000=\frac{2000}{\frac{2500}{B}+0.3} \\\\ & \frac{2500}{B}+0.3=\frac{2000}{5000} \\\\ &am

questions.explanation: Two IP addresses are on the same network if the result of a bitwise AND operation between the IP address and the netmask is identical for both. We need to find which netmask makes 192.168.10.5 and 192.168.12.70 produce the same network ID. Analysis IP A: 192.168.10.5 IP B: 192.168.12.70 The first two octets ( 192.168 ) are identical. The last octet ( .5 and .70 ) is masked by .0 in all options, so it's irrelevant. The decision comes down to the third octet. We need to find a mask that makes 10 and 12 look the same. Let's look at the binary for the third octet: $10=00001010$ $12=00001100$ A. 255.255 .252 .0 Mask ( 252 ): 11111100 IP A: 00001010 AND 11111100 = 00001000 (Network ID: 192.168.8.0) IP B: 00001100 AND 11111100 = 00001100 (Network ID: 192.168.12.0) DIFFERENT. B. 255.255 .254 .0 Mask ( 254 ): 11111110 IPA: 00001010 AND 11111110 = 00001010 (Network ID: 192.168.10.0) IP B: 00001100 AND 11111110 = 00001100 (Network ID: 192.168.12.0) DIFFERENT. C. 255.255 .255 .0 Mask ( 255 ): 111

questions.explanation: Total UDP Segment Size = UDP Header + UDP Payload Total UDP Segment Size = 8 bytes + 4000 bytes = 4008 bytes The total IP packet (header + data) must fit within the 1000-byte MTU. Max IP Packet Size $=1000$ bytes Max Data (IP Payload) in a packet = Max IP Packet Size - IPv4 Header Max Data (IP Payload) in a packet $=1000$ bytes -20 bytes $=980$ bytes A key rule for IPv4 fragmentation is that the data (payload) size of every fragment (except the last one) must be a multiple of 8 to properly state the fragment offset. We check if 980 is a multiple of $8: 980 \div 8=122.5$. It is not. We must find the largest multiple of 8 that is less than or equal to 980. $122 \times 8=976$. Therefore, the maximum data (IP payload) per fragment is 976 bytes. We will fragment the total 4008 bytes of UDP data into chunks of 976 bytes. Total Fragments $=\lceil 4008 \div 976\rceil=\lceil 4.106 \ldots\rceil=5$ fragments. Let's break down the data: Fragment 1: 976 bytes Fragment 2: 976 bytes Fragment 3: 976

questions.questionHtml:
The subnet mask for a particular network is $255.255.240.0$. Which of the following pairs of IP addresses could belong to this network?

  1. $172.16.5.5$ AND $172.17.5.5$
     
  2. $130.20.100.5$ AND $130.20.110.254$
     
  3. $192.168.1.1$ AND $193.168.1.2$
     
  4. $200.10.35.10$ AND $200.10.50.20$
questions.explanation: The first two octets must match exactly (because the mask is 255.255 ). The last octet doesn't matter (because the mask is 0). The third octet is the important one. The mask 240 ( 11110000 ) means the first 4 bits of the third octet must match. A. 172.16.5.5 AND 172.17.5.5 The second octets (16 and 17) do not match. They are on DIFFERENT networks. C. 192.168.1.1 AND 193.168.1.2 The first octets (192 and 193) do not match. They are on DIFFERENT networks. D. 200.10 .35 .10 AND 200.10 .50 .20 The first two octets ( 200.10 ) match. We must check the third octet: 35 and 50 . 35 in binary is 00100011 50 in binary is 00110010 The first 4 bits ( 0010 and 0011 ) do not match. They are on DIFFERENT networks. B. 130.20.100.5 AND 130.20.110.254 The first two octets ( 130.20 ) match. We must check the third octet: 100 and 110 . 100 in binary is 01100100 110 in binary is 01101110 The first 4 bits ( 0110 and 0110 ) are identical. They are on the SAME network. The correct choice is $\mathbf{B}$.

questions.questionHtml:
Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that the IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of 1400 bytes in its data field (MTU). A UDP segment is to be transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 4320 bytes.

Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment, including its IPv4 header?

  1. 3 FRAGMENTS, 1396 BYTES
     
  2. 4 FRAGMENTS, 200 BYTES
     
  3. 4 FRAGMENTS, 220 BYTES
     
  4. 5 FRAGMENTS, 220 BYTES
questions.explanation: Total UDP Segment Size = UDP Header + UDP Payload Total UDP Segment Size = 8 bytes + 4320 bytes = 4328 bytes The total IP packet (header + data) must fit within the 1400-byte MTU. Max IP Packet Size = 1400 bytes Max Data (IP Payload) in a packet = Max IP Packet Size - IPv4 Header Max Data (IP Payload) in a packet $=1400$ bytes -20 bytes $=1380$ bytes However, in IPv4 fragmentation, the fragment offset is measured in 8-byte blocks. This means the data (payload) size of every fragment (except the last one) must be a multiple of 8. We check if 1380 is a multiple of $8: 1380 \div 8=172.5$. It is not. We must find the largest multiple of 8 that is less than or equal to 1380. $172 \times 8=1376$. Therefore, the maximum data (IP payload) per fragment is 1376 bytes. Fragment 1: Data: 1376 bytes Remaining Data: $4328-1376=2952$ bytes Fragment 2: Data: 1376 bytes Remaining Data: 2952-1376 = 1576 bytes Fragment 3: Data: 1376 bytes Remaining Data: $1576-1376=200$ bytes Fragment 4 (Last Fragment):

questions.explanation: When a TCP timeout occurs, the connection takes two immediate actions: 1. The Slow Start Threshold ( ssthresh ) is set to half of the current congestion window ( cwnd ). ssthresh $=64 \mathrm{~KB} / 2=32 \mathrm{~KB}$ 2. The Congestion Window ( cwnd ) is reset to the initial window size, which is 1 Maximum Segment Size (MSS). $\mathrm{cwnd}=1$ * $\mathrm{MSS}=1 \mathrm{~KB}$ The connection now enters the Slow Start phase. Start: cwnd $=1 \mathrm{~KB}$ After 1 RTT (50 msec): cwnd $=1{ }^{\star} 2=2 \mathrm{~KB}$ After 2 RTTs ( 100 msec): cwnd $=2^* 2=4 \mathrm{~KB}$ After 3 RTTs ( 150 msec ): cwnd $=4{ }^* 2=8 \mathrm{~KB}$ After 4 RTTs $(200 \mathrm{msec})$ : cwnd $=8^{\star} 2=16 \mathrm{~KB}$ After 5 RTTs (250 msec): cwnd $=16 * 2=32$ KB At this point, the cwnd ( 32 KB ) has reached the ssthresh ( 32 KB ). This phase is over. Time taken for Slow Start: 5 RTTs * $50 \mathrm{msec} /$ RTT $=250 \mathrm{msec}$ Now that cwnd $\geq$ ssthresh, the connection enters the Congestion Avoidance

The link $\mathbf{Q} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ has a bandwidth of $1 \times 10^6$ bits/sec and a propagation delay of 4 ms . Router $\mathbf{Q}$ is a store-and-forward router. It immediately begins to transmit a packet on link $\mathbf{Q} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ as soon as it has fully received the packet on link $\mathbf{P} \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}$, provided the $\mathbf{Q} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ link is free. Router $\mathbf{Q}$ can simultaneously receive on link $\mathbf{P} \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}$ and transmit on link $\mathbf{Q} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ (i.e., it supports pipelining). Assume $\mathbf{P}$ starts transmitting the first chunk at $t=0$. Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which $\mathbf{R}$ receives the last bit of the entire file? $8.014$ $16.000$ $16.004$ $16.010$

Consider a network path $\mathbf{P} \rightarrow \mathbf{Q} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ between nodes $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ via router $\mathbf{Q}$. Node $\mathbf{P}$ sends a file of $2 \times 10^6$ bytes to $\mathbf{R}$ by splitting the file into chunks of $10^3$ bytes each. Node $\mathbf{P}$ sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible.

The link $\mathbf{P} \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}$ has a bandwidth of $2 \times 10^6$ bits/sec and a propagation delay of 2 ms . The link $\mathbf{Q} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ has a bandwidth of $1 \times 10^6$ bits/sec and a propagation delay of 4 ms .

Router $\mathbf{Q}$ is a store-and-forward router. It immediately begins to transmit a packet on link $\mathbf{Q} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ as soon as it has fully received the packet on link $\mathbf{P} \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}$, provided the $\mathbf{Q} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ link is free. Router $\mathbf{Q}$ can simultaneously receive on link $\mathbf{P} \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}$ and transmit on link $\mathbf{Q} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ (i.e., it supports pipelining).

Assume $\mathbf{P}$ starts transmitting the first chunk at $t=0$.

Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which $\mathbf{R}$ receives the last bit of the entire file?

  1. $8.014$
     
  2. $16.000$
     
  3. $16.004$
     
  4. $16.010$
questions.explanation: The total time is limited by the bottleneck link ( $\mathrm{Q} \rightarrow \mathrm{R}$ ). The total time to transmit the entire file over this link is $N \times T_{x 2}$. However, this link can only start working after the first packet has been transmitted and propagated from $P$. 1. Time for bottleneck to start $=T_{x 1}+P_{d 1}=0.004+0.002=0.006 \mathrm{sec}$. 2. Time for bottleneck to transmit all $N$ packets $=N \times T_{x 2}=2000 \times 0.008=16.0 \mathrm{sec}$. 3. Time for the last bit to propagate from Q to $\mathrm{R}=P_{d 2}=0.004 \mathrm{sec}$. 4. Total Time $=($ Time to fill first stage $)+($ Total time on bottleneck $)+$ (Time to empty last stage) 5. Total Time $=\left(T_{x 1}+P_{d 1}\right)+\left(N \times T_{x 2}\right)+P_{d 2}$ (This formula works because $T_{x 2}>T_{x 1}$ ) 6. Total Time $=(0.004+0.002)+(2000 \times 0.008)+0.004=0.006+16.0+ 0.004=\mathbf{1 6 . 0 1 0} \mathbf{~ s e c}$. GO Classes answered Nov 3, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please lo

questions.questionText: In an IPv4 datagram, the $M$ bit is $\mathbf{1}$, the value of $H L E N$ is $\mathbf{5}$, the value of total length is $\mathbf{1 5 0 0}$ and the fragment offset value is $100$. The position of the datagram and the sequence numbers of the first and the last bytes of the payload, respectively, are: First fragment, $800$ and $2279$ Last fragment, $800$ and $2279$ Middle fragment, $100$ and $1579$ Middle fragment, $800$ and $2279$
questions.questionHtml:
In an IPv4 datagram, the $M$ bit is $\mathbf{1}$, the value of $H L E N$ is $\mathbf{5}$, the value of total length is $\mathbf{1 5 0 0}$ and the fragment offset value is $100$. The position of the datagram and the sequence numbers of the first and the last bytes of the payload, respectively, are:

  1. First fragment, $800$ and $2279$
     
  2. Last fragment, $800$ and $2279$
     
  3. Middle fragment, $100$ and $1579$
     
  4. Middle fragment, $800$ and $2279$
questions.explanation: Position: $M=1$ (more fragments) and Offset > 0 , so it is a Middle fragment. Header Length: $H L E N \times 4=5 \times 4=20$ bytes. Payload Length: Total Length - Header Length = $1500-20=1480$ bytes. First Byte: Fragment Offset $\times 8=100 \times 8=800$. Last Byte: First Byte + Payload Length $-1=800+1480-1=2279$. questions.explanation: 254 Om Dwivedi answered Oct 29, 2025 Om Dwivedi comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes In Class C IPv4 addressing, 24 bits are assigned for the Network ID , and 8 bits are assigned for the Host ID . So, the total number of host addresses possible within a single Class C network is: 2^8=256 However, 2 addresses are reserved : One for the Network Address (all host bits = 0) One for the Broadcast Address (all host bits = 1) Hence, the number of usable host addresses is: 2^8 -  2=254 Satyendra_Gautam answered Oct 29, 2025 Satyendra_Gautam comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Class C network → Default subnet mask: 255.255.255.0 Host portion → 8 bits Total addresses → 2^{8} = 256 Reserved addresses : Network address (all host bits = 0) → e.g., 192.168.1.0 Broadcast address (all host bits = 1) → e.g., 192.168.1.255 Usable host addresses → 256−2= 254 Sahdev answered Oct 30, 2025 Sahdev comment

questions.questionText: Consider the resolution of the domain name www.research.ac.uk by a local DNS resolver using an iterative query mechanism. Assume the resolver's cache is not empty; it already contains the resource record for the .ac.uk name server. No other records are cached. The number of new external DNS query-response pairs the resolver must initiate to find the IP address is $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.questionHtml: Consider the resolution of the domain name www.research.ac.uk by a local DNS resolver using an iterative query mechanism. Assume the resolver's cache is not empty; it already contains the resource record for the .ac.uk name server. No other records are cached. The number of new external DNS query-response pairs the resolver must initiate to find the IP address is $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.explanation: The iterative process performed by the resolver is as follows: 1. The resolver checks its cache and finds the address for the .ac. uk server. This allows it to skip querying the Root server and the .uk TLD server. 2. Resolver asks the .ac.uk server for www.research.ac.uk. The server replies with the address of the research.ac.uk server. (External Pair 1) 3. Resolver asks the research.ac.uk (authoritative) server for www.research.ac.uk. The server replies with the final IP address. (External Pair 2) This requires a total of 2 external query-response pairs. (This count does not include the initial query from the user's computer to the local resolver). questions.questionHtml: A web browser, with an empty cache, is set to use persistent HTTP and can open up to $6$ parallel connections to a single server. A requested web page contains one main HTML file and $10$ embedded images (all hosted on the same server). What is the minimum number of TCP connections the browser will open to display the page completely?
questions.explanation: The browser will open its maximum number of parallel connections ($6$) to the server. It will download the HTML file on one connection and then distribute the $10$ image requests across those same $6$ persistent connections as they become available. All $11$ objects are multiplexed over these $6$ connections, which are opened once and then reused. questions.questionText: A network administrator is configuring four devices: a server (S), a printer (P), a workstation (W). and a router's interface (R). Their IP addresses are assigned as follows: Server (S): $192.168.50.78$ Printer (P): $192.168.50.97$ Workstation (W): $192.168.50.65$ Router (R): $192.168.50.94$ All devices are configured with the subnet mask 255.255.255.224. Which of the following statements accurately describes the network configuration? The Server, Workstation, and Router are on the same subnet, but the Printer is on a different one. The Server and Printer are on one subnet, and the Workstation and Router are on another. All four devices are on the same subnet. The Printer and Router are on the same subnet, but the Server and Workstation are on different subnets.
questions.questionHtml:
A network administrator is configuring four devices: a server (S), a printer (P), a workstation (W). and a router's interface (R). Their IP addresses are assigned as follows:

  • Server (S): $192.168.50.78$
     
  • Printer (P): $192.168.50.97$
     
  • Workstation (W): $192.168.50.65$
     
  • Router (R): $192.168.50.94$

All devices are configured with the subnet mask 255.255.255.224. Which of the following statements accurately describes the network configuration?

  1. The Server, Workstation, and Router are on the same subnet, but the Printer is on a different one.
     
  2. The Server and Printer are on one subnet, and the Workstation and Router are on another.
     
  3. All four devices are on the same subnet.
     
  4. The Printer and Router are on the same subnet, but the Server and Workstation are on different subnets.

options.label: A
options.text: The Server, Workstation, and Router are on the same subnet, but the Printer is on a different one.

options.label: B
options.text: The Server and Printer are on one subnet, and the Workstation and Router are on another.

options.label: C
options.text: All four devices are on the same subnet.

options.label: D
options.text: The Printer and Router are on the same subnet, but the Server and Workstation are on different subnets.

questions.explanation: The key to this problem is the subnet mask: 255.255 .255 .224 . The first three octets ( 255.255 .255 ) are straightforward. The last octet, 224 , is where the division happens. In binary, 224 is 11100000 . This means the first 3 bits of the last octet are used for the network address, and the last 5 bits are for host addresses. The "magic number" or block size for this subnet mask is $256-224=32$. This means our subnets will be in blocks of 32 addresses. Starting from 0 , we can map out the subnets for the $192.168 .50 . x$ network: Subnet 1: 192.168.50.0 (Network ID) to 192.168.50.31 (Broadcast ID) Subnet 2: 192.168 .50 .32 to 192.168 .50 .63 Subnet 3: 192.168 .50 .64 to 192.168 .50 .95 Subnet 4: 192.168 .50 .96 to 192.168 .50 .127  ... and so on. Now, we just need to see which range each device's IP address falls into: Server (S): 192.168.50.78 78 is between 64 and 95 , so it's in Subnet 3. Workstation (W): 192.168.50.65 65 is between 64 and 95, so it's in Subnet 3. Router (R)

questions.questionText: A network router uses the token bucket algorithm to manage outgoing traffic. The bucket has a capacity of $500$ tokens, where each token corresponds to one packet. Tokens are generated and added to the bucket at a constant rate of $200$ per second. The router can transmit packets at a maximum rate of $800$ packets per second as long as there are tokens in the bucket. If the bucket is initially half-full and a burst of $2000$ packets arrives to be transmitted, the minimum time required to send all $2000$ packets is $\_\_\_\_$ seconds.
questions.questionHtml:
A network router uses the token bucket algorithm to manage outgoing traffic. The bucket has a capacity of $500$ tokens, where each token corresponds to one packet. Tokens are generated and added to the bucket at a constant rate of $200$ per second. The router can transmit packets at a maximum rate of $800$ packets per second as long as there are tokens in the bucket.

If the bucket is initially half-full and a burst of $2000$ packets arrives to be transmitted, the minimum time required to send all $2000$ packets is $\_\_\_\_$ seconds.
questions.explanation: The formula you used. $M=(c+\rho \cdot t) / t$, helps find the time $(t)$ for which the router can sustain its maximum output rate ( $M$ ) before the initial credit ( $c$ ) of tokens is exhausted. Your calculation is perfectly correct: $$ \begin{gathered} 800=\frac{250+200 \cdot t}{t} \\ 800 t=250+200 t \\ 600 t=250 \\ t=\frac{250}{600}=\frac{5}{12} \text { seconds } \end{gathered} $$ This is the duration of the initial burst. Now, to get the total time, we just need to complete the final steps. During this initial burst of $5 / 12$ seconds, the router was sending at its maximum speed of 800 packets/second. Packets sent: $800 \frac{\text { packets }}{\mathrm{sec}} \times \frac{5}{12} \mathrm{sec}=\frac{4000}{12}=\frac{1000}{3}$ packets. Now, we find how many packets are left and how long it takes to send them at the sustained rate. Packets remaining: $2000-\frac{1000}{3}=\frac{6000-1000}{3}=\frac{5000}{3}$ packets. The connection starts with a congestion window ( cwnd ) of $1$ MSS and an initial slow start threshold ( ssthresh ) of $32$ MSS. questions.questionHtml:
A TCP connection is used for a critical file transfer. The connection starts with a congestion window ( cwnd ) of $1$ MSS and an initial slow start threshold ( ssthresh ) of $32$ MSS. The transfer proceeds smoothly until the network detects congestion during the $7$th transmission round, signalled by the receipt of three duplicate ACKs.

Following this event, what will the size of the congestion window be at the conclusion of the $11$th transmission round?

  1. $16$ MSS
     
  2. $18$ MSS
     
  3. $20$ MSS
     
  4. $32$ MSS
questions.explanation: The connection begins in the Slow Start phase since the initial cwnd (1 MSS) is less than the ssthresh ( 32 MSS). In this phase, cwnd doubles after each successful transmission round. Initial: cwnd =1, ssthresh=32 After Tx 1: cwnd =1*2=2 After Tx 2: cwnd $=2^* 2=4$ After Tx 3: cwnd $=4^{\star} 2=8$ After Tx 4: cwnd $=8^* 2=16$ After Tx 5: cwnd $=16^* 2=32$. At this point, cwnd reaches ssthresh. The connection now switches to the Congestion Avoidance phase. After Tx 6: In Congestion Avoidance, cwnd increases by 1. So, cwnd $=32+1=33$ MSS. During the 7th transmission, three duplicate ACKs are received. This signals congestion but not a complete packet loss, triggering a "fast recovery" mechanism. 1. The ssthresh is updated to half of the current cwnd (which was 33 MSS). New ssthresh = floor(33 / 2) = $\mathbf{1 6}$ MSS. 2. The cwnd is set to the new ssthresh value. questions.questionHtml:
A TCP connection is operating using the Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD) algorithm. At the beginning of the connection, the congestion window ( cwnd ) is set to $1$ MSS and the slow start threshold ( ssthresh ) is $16$ MSS. The connection proceeds normally until a timeout occurs during the sixth round of transmission.

What will be the size of the congestion window at the end of the twelfth transmission round?

  1. $8$ MSS
     
  2. $10$ MSS
     
  3. $11$ MSS
     
  4. $12$ MSS
questions.explanation: Initially, the connection is in the Slow Start phase because the cwnd (1 MSS) is less than the ssthresh ( 16 MSS). In this phase, the cwnd doubles after each successful transmission. Initial: cwnd =1, ssthresh=16 After Tx 1: cwnd $=1^* 2=2$ After Tx 2: cwnd $=2 * 2=4$ After Tx 3: cwnd $=4 * 2=8$ After Tx 4: cwnd $=8^* 2=16$. At this point, cwnd reaches ssthresh, so the connection switches to the Congestion Avoidance phase for the next transmission. In Congestion Avoidance, cwnd increases by just 1 MSS per transmission (additively). After Tx 5: cwnd $=16+1=17$ A timeout occurs during the 6th transmission. This is a severe event, triggering the following actions: 1. The ssthresh is set to half of the current cwnd . New ssthresh $=$ floor $(17 / 2)=8$ MSS. 2. The cwnd is reset to 1 MSS. 3. The connection goes back into the Slow Start phase. Now, we trace the cwnd from its reset state. State after timeout: cwnd $=1$, ssthresh $=8$ Slow Start Phase (again): After Tx 7: cwnd $=1^* 2=2$ Afte

A university department is setting up a new network that uses the CSMA/CD protocol for media access. The network operates at a bandwidth of $100$ Mbps. The design specifies that the minimum size for any frame sent on the network is $128$ bytes. The signal propagation speed through the network cable is $2 \times 10^8$ meters/second.

questions.questionText: A client and server establish a TCP connection. The connection has the following characteristics: the round trip time (RTT) is $10$ ms , the slow-start threshold is initially $24$ KB , the receiver's advertised window is $60$ KB, and the maximum segment size (MSS) is $1$ KB . The connection starts at time $t=0$. Assume the connection is always active and there are no packet losses or timeouts. The size of the congestion window (in KB) at time $t=70 \mathrm{~ms}$ will be $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.questionHtml:
A client and server establish a TCP connection. The connection has the following characteristics: the round trip time (RTT) is $10$ ms , the slow-start threshold is initially $24$ KB , the receiver's advertised window is $60$ KB, and the maximum segment size (MSS) is $1$ KB . The connection starts at time $t=0$. Assume the connection is always active and there are no packet losses or timeouts.

The size of the congestion window (in KB) at time $t=70 \mathrm{~ms}$ will be $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.explanation: RTT: $10$ ms ssthresh : $24$ KB MSS: $1$ KB The cwnd starts at $1$ KB and doubles every $10$ ms. $\mathrm{t}=0 \mathrm{~ms}:$ cwnd $=1 \mathrm{~KB}$ $\mathrm{t}=10 \mathrm{~ms}:$ cwnd $=2 \mathrm{~KB}$ $\mathrm{t}=20 \mathrm{~ms}:$ cwnd $=4 \mathrm{~KB}$ $\mathrm{t}=30 \mathrm{~ms}: \mathrm{cwnd}=8 \mathrm{~KB}$ $\mathrm{t}=40 \mathrm{~ms}: \mathrm{cwnd}^{-}=16 \mathrm{~KB}$ $\mathbf{t = 5 0 ~ m s}$ : At the previous step, cwnd was $16$ KB . Doubling it would be $32$ KB . Since $32$ KB is greater than the ssthresh of 24 KB , the cwnd is instead set to the ssthresh value. $\mathrm{cwnd}=24 \mathrm{~KB}$ The connection switches to congestion avoidance. The cwnd now increases by 1 MSS ( 1 KB) every RTT. $\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{6 0 ~ m s}:$ cwnd $=24 \mathrm{~KB}+1 \mathrm{~KB}=\mathbf{2 5} \mathbf{~ K B}$. $\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{7 0} \mathbf{~ m s}:$ cwnd $=25 \mathrm{~KB}+1 \mathrm{~KB}=\mathbf{2 6} \mathbf{~ K B}$. Each host always has data to send and attempts to transmit in any given time slot with a probability of $p=$ 0.25 . questions.questionHtml:
In a time-slotted MAC protocol system, there are 5 hosts competing for the channel. Each host always has data to send and attempts to transmit in any given time slot with a probability of $p=$ 0.25 . There is no backoff, and a collision occurs if more than one host transmits simultaneously.

What is the overall efficiency of the channel, defined as the probability that a time slot contains exactly one successful transmission?

  1. $0.250$
     
  2. $0.316$
     
  3. $0.395$
     
  4. $0.781$
questions.explanation: The formula for total channel efficiency in a slotted ALOHA system is $S=N \cdot p \cdot(1-p)^{N-1}$. 1. Plug in the values: Number of hosts $(N)=5$ Transmission probability $(p)=0.25$ Non-transmission probability $(1-p)=0.75$ 2. Calculate: $S=5 \cdot(0.25) \cdot(0.75)^{5-1}$ $S=1.25 \cdot(0.75)^4$ $S=1.25 \cdot 0.3164$ $S \approx 0.3955$ This matches option C. 0.395. questions.questionText: The processing engine of a new router is benchmarked and found to have a maximum, fixed processing time of $0.5376$ microseconds for any single packet. The router is being equipped with a new full-duplex interface and must be able to forward a continuous stream of minimum-sized Ethernet frames (totalling $84$ bytes on the wire, including all overhead) without dropping any. What is the minimum link speed that the new interface must support to allow for wirespeed forwarding? $100 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s}$ $1000 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s}$ $1250 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s}$ $2500 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s}$
questions.questionHtml:
The processing engine of a new router is benchmarked and found to have a maximum, fixed processing time of $0.5376$ microseconds for any single packet. The router is being equipped with a new full-duplex interface and must be able to forward a continuous stream of minimum-sized Ethernet frames (totalling $84$ bytes on the wire, including all overhead) without dropping any.

What is the minimum link speed that the new interface must support to allow for wirespeed forwarding?

  1. $100 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s}$
     
  2. $1000 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s}$
     
  3. $1250 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s}$
     
  4. $2500 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s}$
questions.explanation: Understand the Wirespeed Condition: For wirespeed forwarding, the router must finish processing a packet before the next one fully arrives. Therefore, the minimum time to transmit a packet on the wire must be equal to the router's maximum processing time. Processing Time $=0.5376$ microseconds $(\mu s)=0.5376 \times 10^{-6}$ seconds. Calculate the total minimum frame size in bits: Total Size = 84 bytes. Total Bits $=84$ bytes * 8 bits/byte $=672$ bits. Calculate the required link speed: The required speed is the number of bits in the packet divided by the maximum time allowed to process it. Link Speed = Total Bits / Processing Time Link Speed $=672$ bits $/\left(0.5376 \times 10^{-6} s\right)=1,250,000,000$ bits per second. Convert to Mb/s (Megabits per second): Link Speed $=1,250,000,000 / 1,000,000=1250 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s}$. questions.questionHtml:
A line card on a modern switch has several Gigabit Ethernet ports, each operating at $1 \mathrm{~Gb} / \mathrm{s}\left(10^9\right.$ bits per second). The switch must be able to handle a continuous "worst-case" stream of minimum-sized Ethernet frames without any drops. For this calculation, assume a minimum frame on the wire consists of a $64$-byte frame, an $8$-byte preamble, and a $12$-byte Inter-Packet Gap (IPG).

What is the theoretical forwarding rate (in Millions of packets per second, Mpps) that a single port's processing logic must support to achieve wirespeed performance?

  1. $0.148$ Mpps
     
  2. $1.488$ Mpps
     
  3. $8.125$ Mpps
     
  4. $14.880$ Mpps
questions.explanation: Calculate the total minimum frame size in bits: The total size on the wire includes the frame, preamble, and the Inter-Packet-Gap (IPG). Total Size = 64 bytes (frame) + 8 bytes (preamble) + 12 bytes (IPG) = 84 bytes. Total Bits $=84$ bytes * 8 bits/byte $=672$ bits. Calculate the time to transmit one packet: This is determined by how many bits the $1 \mathrm{~Gb} / \mathrm{s}$ link can transmit per second. Link Speed = $1 \mathrm{~Gb} / \mathrm{s}=1 \times 10^9$ bits per second. Time per Packet = Total Bits / Link Speed = 672 bits / $\left(1 \times 10^9 \mathrm{~b} / \mathrm{s}\right)=672 \times 10^{-9}$ seconds. Calculate the packet rate (Packets Per Second): The forwarding rate is the reciprocal of the time per packet. Packets Per Second (PPS) $=1 /$ Time per Packet $=1 /\left(672 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~s}\right) \approx 1,488,095$ PPS. Convert to Mpps (Millions of packets per second): Mpps $=1,488,095 / 1,000,000 \approx 1.488$ Mpps. GO Classes answered Oct 22, 2025 GO Classes com

questions.questionText: A communication channel over a transatlantic fiber-optic link is managed using a selective repeat sliding window protocol. The protocol uses a frame size of 2 KB to send data over the 10 Mbps link, which has a one-way propagation delay of 40 msec . To achieve a minimum link utilization of $80 \%$, the minimum number of bits required for the sequence number field is $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.questionHtml: A communication channel over a transatlantic fiber-optic link is managed using a selective repeat sliding window protocol. The protocol uses a frame size of 2 KB to send data over the 10 Mbps link, which has a one-way propagation delay of 40 msec . To achieve a minimum link utilization of $80 \%$, the minimum number of bits required for the sequence number field is $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.explanation: It is given that Bandwidth ($B$) = $10 \text{ Mbps}$ Propagation Delay ($T_p$) = $40 \text{ ms}$ Frame Size ($L$) = $2 \text{ KB} $ Transmission Delay ($T_t$) = $\frac{L}{B} = \frac{16000}{10^7} = 1.6 \text{ ms}$ $$a = \frac{T_p}{T_t} = \frac{40 \text{ ms}}{1.6 \text{ ms}} = 25$$ Finding Window Size ($N$): Using the efficiency formula $\eta = \frac{N}{1 + 2a}$ where N is the window size of both the sender and receiver (because sender and receiver have same window size in selective repeat) $$0.8 \leq \frac{N}{1 + 2(25)}$$ $$0.8 \leq \frac{N}{51}$$ $$N \geq 0.8 \times 51$$ $$N \geq 40.8$$ Minimum sender window size ($W_s$) = $41$. In Selective Repeat, the sequence number space must be at least the sum of the sender and receiver windows ($2^n \geq W_s + W_r$). Assuming $W_s = W_r$: $$2^n \geq 41 + 41$$ $$2^n \geq 82$$ $$n = \lceil \log_2(82) \rceil = 7$$ Answer:$7$ Sudeep 1 answered Feb 12 Sudeep 1 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation: \[ BW = 100~\text{Mbps} = 100 \times 10^6~\text{bps}, \quad d = 200~\text{m}, \quad v = 2 \times 10^8~\text{m/s} \] \[ \textbf{1. Propagation delay (one-way):} \quad T_p = \frac{d}{v} = \frac{200}{2 \times 10^8} = 1 \times 10^{-6}~\text{s} = 1~\mu s \] \[ \textbf{2. questions.questionHtml:
A server ( S ) sends a 4 Megabit ( $4 \times 10^{6}$ bits) file to a client (D). The path between S and D consists of three routers, creating a total of four links. The file is segmented into 2000 packets of equal size. Each of the four links has a length of 200 km and a bandwidth of 10 Mbps . If the signal propagation speed over the links is $2 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, what is the total end-to-end delay to send the entire file? (Assume there is no queuing or processing delay).

A. 400 ms

B. 404 ms

C. 1600 ms

D. 1604 ms
questions.explanation: the total time for the first packet to make the complete journey is: $4 \times T_{\text {trans }}+4 \times T_{\text {prop }}$ Time $=4 \times 0.2 \mathrm{~ms}+4 \times 1 \mathrm{~ms}=0.8 \mathrm{~ms}+4 \mathrm{~ms}=4.8 \mathrm{~ms}$ There are 2000 packets in total. After the first one is sent, there are still 1999 packets left to be transmitted by the source. The time required for this is: Additional Time = 1999 packets $\times T_{\text {trans }} /$ packet Additional Time $=1999 \times 0.2 \mathrm{~ms}=399.8 \mathrm{~ms}$ Total Time $=($ Time for 1 st packet $)+($ Time for rest of packets $)$ Total Time $=4.8 \mathrm{~ms}+399.8 \mathrm{~ms}=404.6 \mathrm{~ms}$ Hence $B$ is correct

questions.questionHtml: Suppose the congestion window size of a TCP connection is $60$ KB when a timeout occurs. The connection has a round trip time of $50$ msec and uses a maximum segment size of $3$ KB . The time taken (in msec) by the TCP connection to reach a $60$ KB congestion window again is $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.explanation: cwnd at timeout $=60 \mathrm{~KB} / 3 \mathrm{~KB} / \mathrm{MSS}=20 \mathrm{MSS}$. Target cwnd $=60 \mathrm{~KB} / 3 \mathrm{~KB} / \mathrm{MSS}=20 \mathrm{MSS}$. RTT $=50 \mathrm{msec}$. When the timeout occurs at cwnd $=20$ MSS: The new slow start threshold ( ssthresh ) is set to half of the current cwnd . ssthresh $=\frac{20}{2}=10 \mathrm{MSS}$ The cwnd is reset to 1 MSS. The connection enters the Slow Start phase. The goal is to increase the cwnd from 1 MSS to the new ssthresh of 10 MSS. In this phase, the cwnd doubles every RTT. Start: cwnd $=1$ MSS After 1 RTT ( 50 ms ): cwnd $=2$ MSS After 2 RTTs $(100 \mathrm{~ms})$ : cwnd $=4$ MSS After 3 RTTs ( 150 ms ): cwnd $=8$ MSS After 4 RTTs $(200 \mathrm{~ms})$ : cwnd would double to 16 MSS , but since this is greater than the ssthresh of 10 MSS, the cwnd is instead set to 10 MSS. The Slow Start phase is now complete. Time taken for Slow Start: 4 RTTs $=4 \times 50 \mathrm{msec}=200 \mathrm{msec}$. At this point, the cwnd is 10 MSS.

The aggregate number of transmissions (including new and retransmitted frames) is modelled as a Poisson process with a rate of $250$ frames per second. What is the throughput of the network in frames per second (rounded to the nearest integer)?
questions.questionHtml:
A network uses the pure ALOHA protocol where each frame is $2,000$ bits long. The channel transmission rate is $1$ Mbps ( $=10^6$ bits per second). The aggregate number of transmissions (including new and retransmitted frames) is modelled as a Poisson process with a rate of $250$ frames per second.

What is the throughput of the network in frames per second (rounded to the nearest integer)?
questions.explanation: Frame Transmission Time ( $T_{f r}$ ): $$ T_{f r}=\frac{\text { Frame Length }}{\text { Channel Rate }}=\frac{2,000 \text { bits }}{1,000,000 \mathrm{bps}}=0.002 \text { seconds } $$ Offered Load (G): $$ \begin{aligned} & G=\text { Attempt } \operatorname{Rate}(\lambda) \times T_{f r} \\ & G=250 \text { frames } / \mathrm{s} \times 0.002 \mathrm{~s}=0.5 \end{aligned} $$ The normalized throughput (S) is calculated using the formula $S=G \cdot e^{-2 G}$ : $$ \begin{aligned} & S=0.5 \times e^{-2(0.5)} \\ & S=0.5 \times e^{-1} \\ & S \approx 0.184 \end{aligned} $$ This result (S) is then multiplied by the attempt rate ( $\lambda$ ): $$ \begin{aligned} & \text { Result }=S \times \lambda \\ & \text { Result }=0.184 \times 250 \end{aligned} $$ The final answer is 46. questions.questionHtml:
A host needs to send a large UDP datagram over a network that uses IPv4. The network link has an MTU of $1492$ bytes. The UDP segment contains $4400$ bytes of application data. Assuming the IPv4 header does not contain any optional fields, which of the following correctly states the total number of fragments generated and the total size of the final fragment?

  1. $3$ fragments, $1476$ bytes
     
  2. $3$ fragments, $1484$ bytes
     
  3. $2$ fragments, $1484$ bytes
     
  4. $3$ fragments, $1464$ bytes
questions.explanation: 1. Calculate Total IP Payload: The data that the IP layer needs to fragment is the entire UDP segment. Total IP Payload = (UDP Data) + (UDP Header) Total IP Payload = 4400 bytes + 8 bytes = 4408 bytes 2. Calculate Maximum Data per Fragment: The maximum data in a fragment is the MTU minus the IP header size. Max Data = MTU - IPv4 Header Max Data = 1492 bytes - 20 bytes = 1472 bytes (Note: 1472 is a multiple of 8 , so we can use this full size). 3. Determine the Fragments: We need to send 4408 bytes of data, with each full fragment carrying 1472 bytes. Fragment 1: carries 1472 bytes. (Remaining data: 4408-1472 = 2936 bytes) Fragment 2: carries 1472 bytes. (Remaining data: 2936-1472 = 1464 bytes) Fragment 3 (Final): carries the leftover 1464 bytes of data. This gives a total of $\mathbf{3}$ fragments. 4. Calculate the Total Size of the Final Fragment: This is the crucial last step. The total size includes the data and the header. Total Size $=($ Data in last fragment $)+($ IPv4 Header $)
