A $1$ Mbps satellite link with a one-way propagation delay of $45$ ms uses the Go-Back-N protocol. If the data frames are $1$ Kilobyte ($1024$ bytes) in size, what is the minimum sender window size required to achieve a channel utilization of at least $60 \%$ ? (Assume ACK frames have negligible transmission time).

  1. $7$
     
  2. $8$
     
  3. $11$
     
  4. $12$
questions.explanation: Bandwidth $(\mathrm{B})=1 \mathrm{Mbps}=10^6 \mathrm{bits} / \mathrm{sec}$ Frame Size $(\mathrm{L})=1 \mathrm{~KB}=1024$ bytes $=8192$ bits Propagation Delay $\left(T_p\right)=45 \mathrm{~ms}=0.045 \mathrm{sec}$ Required Efficiency $(\eta) \geq 60 \%$ or 0.6 Window Size $(\mathrm{W})=$ ? Calculate Transmission Time $\left(T_t\right)$ : This is the time to put one frame on the wire. $T_t=L / B=8192$ bits $/ 10^6$ bits $/ \mathrm{sec}=0.008192 \mathrm{sec}$ Use the Efficiency Formula for Go-Back-N: $\eta=\left(W \times T_t\right) /\left(T_t+2 \times T_p\right)$ Solve for $W$ : $0.6 \leq(W \times 0.008192) /(0.008192+2 \times 0.045)$ $0.6 \leq(W \times 0.008192) /(0.008192+0.09)$ $0.6 \leq(W \times 0.008192) / 0.098192$ $0.6 \times 0.098192 \leq W \times 0.008192$ $0.0589152 \leq W \times 0.008192$ $W \geq 0.0589152 / 0.008192$ $W \geq 7.19 \ldots$ Since the window size must be an integer, the minimum required size is $8$ . questions.questionHtml:
A CSMA/CD network operates at $100$ Mbps ( $10^8$ bits per second) over a $2.5$ km cable without any repeaters. The signal propagation speed in the cable is $2 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}$. What is the minimum required frame size for this network in bytes?

  1. $25000$
     
  2. $3125$
     
  3. $5000$
     
  4. $6250$
questions.explanation: Calculate the Propagation Delay $\left(T_p\right)$ : This is the time it takes for a signal to travel the length of the cable. Distance $=2.5 \mathrm{~km}=2500 \mathrm{~m}$ Signal Speed $=2 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}$ $T_p=$ Distance $/$ Signal Speed $T_p=2500 /\left(2 \times 10^7\right)=1.25 \times 10^{-4}$ seconds. Calculate the Round Trip Time (RTT): For collision detection in CSMA/CD, the signal must travel to the end of the cable and back. RTT $=2 \times T_p$ RTT $=2 \times 1.25 \times 10^{-4}=2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ seconds. Find the Minimum Transmission Time ( $T_t$ ): The rule in CSMA/CD is that the transmission time for the smallest frame must be at least the RTT. $T_{t(\min )}=R T T=2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ seconds. Calculate the Minimum Frame Size (L): Bandwidth $=100 \mathrm{Mbps}=10^8$ bits per second $\mathrm{L}=T_{t(\text { min })} \times$ Bandwidth $\mathrm{L}=\left(2.5 \times 10^{-4}\right) \times\left(10^8\right)=25000$ bits. Convert to Bytes: Size in Bytes = 2500

questions.explanation: (B)100 pkts dropper answered Oct 7, 2025 dropper comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply Shanmukhagate commented Nov 19, 2025 reply Follow flag optimal window size =  ( bandwidth * RTT ) / packet size Bandwidth product = bandwidht * RTT = 512 * 10^3 bps * 0.1s packet size = 512 bits Wopt = 100 packets 0 0 reply Share Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes The "optimal window size" is the size needed to achieve $100\%$ efficiency ( $\eta=1$ ). This means the sender can transmit packets continuously without ever stopping to wait for an acknowledgment, thus fully utilizing the bandwidth. The formula for the efficiency of a sliding window protocol is: $$ \eta=\frac{N}{1+2 a} $$ Where: $N=$ Window size in packets. $a=$ The ratio of propagation delay to transmission delay ( $a=\frac{T_p}{T_t}$ ). For maximum throughput, we set efficiency $\eta=1$ : $$ 1=\frac{N}{1+2 a} \Longrightarrow N=1+2 a $$ Our goal is to find the values for $a$ and then solve for $N$.

questions.explanation: Each host needs to generate $500$ unique identifiers per second, which requires $\lceil\lg 500\rceil=9$ bits. Now, these $9$ bits, along with the $32$ bit globally unique IP address, will give a globally unique $41$ bit ID which stays constant. Since we are allowed $52$ bits, we can use the next $11$ bits using the clock, which changes every second. Thus our IDs will wrap around once in $2^{11}=2048$ seconds. Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including the $\mathrm{IPv4}$ header? $7$ fragments, $128$ bytes $6$ fragments, $1608$ bytes $7$ fragments, $148$ bytes $7$ fragments, $156$ bytes
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a network that uses Ethernet and $\mathrm{IPv4}$. Assume that $\mathrm{IPv4}$ headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of $1500$ bytes in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is $9000$ bytes.

Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including the $\mathrm{IPv4}$ header?

  1. $7$ fragments, $128$ bytes
     
  2. $6$ fragments, $1608$ bytes
     
  3. $7$ fragments, $148$ bytes
     
  4. $7$ fragments, $156$ bytes
questions.explanation: $\textbf{Given:}$ Each Ethernet frame data field max = \(1500\) bytes.   IPv4 header (no options) = \(20\) bytes.   UDP payload (data) = \(9000\) bytes.  (Note: the IP payload must carry the entire UDP segment, i.e. UDP header \(8\) bytes + UDP data.) $\textbf{Compute IP payload size (UDP segment length):}$ \[ \text{IP payload} = \text{UDP header} + \text{UDP data} = 8 + 9000 = 9008\ \text{bytes}. \] $\textbf{Maximum data per IP fragment:}$ \[ \text{Max data per fragment} = 1500 - 20 = 1480\ \text{bytes}. \] IPv4 fragment offsets are in 8-byte units, so the fragment data (except final) must be a multiple of 8.   \[ 1480/8 = 185 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 185\times 8 = 1480\ \text{bytes (already a multiple of 8)}. \] $\textbf{Number of fragments:}$ Full fragments of \(1480\) bytes: compute how many fit into \(9008\): \[ \Big\lfloor \frac{9008}{1480} \Big\rfloor = 6,\qquad 6\times1480 = 8880. \] Remaining data for the last fragment: \[ 9008 - 8880 = 128\ \text{bytes}. \]

Which one of the following CIDR prefixes exactly represents the range of IP addresses $172.16.8.0$ to $172.16 .15 .255$ ?

  1. $172.16.8.0 / 24$
     
  2. $172.16.0.0 / 21$
     
  3. $172.16.8.0 / 20$

questions.explanation: The key is to look at the start and end addresses in binary, specifically focusing on the octet where the range begins and ends (the third octet in this case). Start Address (third octet): $8=00001000$ End Address (third octet): $15=00001111$ When you compare them, you can see the first 5 bits ( 00001 ) are identical. The rest of the bits differ, which defines the range for the host addresses. The prefix length is the number of constant bits: 8 bits (from 172 ) +8 bits (from 16 ) +5 bits (from the third octet) $=21$ bits. This gives us a prefix of $\mathbf{/ 2 1}$. The network address is always the first address in the range. In this case, the range is defined to start at $172.16 .8 .0$ , which perfectly matches the prefix we found. Combining the network address and the prefix length gives you the final answer: $$ 172.16 .8 .0 / 21 \text {. } $$ GO Classes answered Sep 29, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Consider three IP networks $A, B$, and $C$. Host $H \_A$ in network $A$ sends messages each containing $240$ bytes of application data to a host $H_{-} C$ in network $C$. The TCP layer prefixes a $20$ byte header to the message.

This passes through an intermediate network $B$. The maximum packet size, including the $20$ byte IP header, in each network is:

  • A: 1500 bytes
     
  • B: 120 bytes
     
  • C: 1500 bytes

The network $A$ and $B$ are connected through a 2 Mbps link, while $B$ and $C$ are connected by a $1$ Mbps link (bps = bits per second).

What is the rate at which application data is transferred to host $H_C$ ? Ignore errors, acknowledgments, and other overheads.

  1. $1.0$ Mbps
     
  2. $1.5$ Mbps
     
  3. $2.0$ Mbps
     
  4. $0.75$ Mbps
questions.explanation: To send one 240-byte application message... - ...we had to transmit a total of $\mathbf{3 2 0}$ bytes across the network (due to fragmentation and the addition of three 20-byte IP headers and one 20-byte TCP header). The efficiency is the ratio of application data to the total data transmitted: Efficiency $=\frac{\text { Application Data }}{\text { Total Transmitted Data }}=\frac{240 \text { bytes }}{320 \text { bytes }}=0.75$ or $\mathbf{7 5} \%$ This means only $75\%$ of the data travelling through the bottleneck link is the actual application data you care about. Application Data Rate $=1 \mathrm{Mbps} \times 0.75=0.75 \mathrm{Mbps}$ GO Classes answered Sep 29, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Professor Rao is explaining TCP congestion control to his students. He presents the following scenario:

  • A TCP sender is operating in the slow start phase.
     
  • The Maximum Segment Size (MSS) $=1000$ bytes.
     
  • Immediately after the $10^{th}$ ACK, the Congestion Window (CWND) is $2000$ bytes.
     
  • With this window, the sender transmits packets $11$ and $12$.
     
  • Now, the ACK for packet $11$ arrives.

According to TCP slow start rules, which new packets will the sender transmit at this point?

  1. Packet $13$ only
     
  2. Packets $13$ and $14$
     
  3. Packets $13, 14,15$
     
  4. None (the sender must wait for more ACKs)

options.label: D
options.text: None (the sender must wait for more ACKs)

questions.explanation: At CWND = $2000$ bytes, the sender can keep $2$ packets in flight $\rightarrow$ packets $11$ and $12$. When ACK for packet $11$ arrives, CWND increases by $\mathbf{+ 1}$ MSS ( $1000$ bytes) $\rightarrow$ CWND $=$ $3000$ bytes. A $3000$-byte window allows $3$ packets in flight. Since packet $12$ is still outstanding, there is room for $\mathbf{2}$ more transmissions $\rightarrow$ packets $\mathbf{1 3}$ and $\mathbf{1 4}$. questions.questionText: If a TCP sender has $14,600$ bytes of data in-flight (i.e., it has sent those bytes but has not yet received acknowledgment for any of them), which of these statements is NOT NECESSARILY true? The congestion window size of the sender is at least $10$ MSS's (or, $14,600$ bytes) The congestion window size of the receiver is at least $10$ MSS's (or, $14,600$ bytes) The sender is expecting acknowledgment packets from the receiver The flow control window advertised by the receiver to the sender is at least $14,600$ bytes
questions.questionHtml:
If a TCP sender has $14,600$ bytes of data in-flight (i.e., it has sent those bytes but has not yet received acknowledgment for any of them), which of these statements is NOT NECESSARILY true?

  1. The congestion window size of the sender is at least $10$ MSS's (or, $14,600$ bytes)
     
  2. The congestion window size of the receiver is at least $10$ MSS's (or, $14,600$ bytes)
     
  3. The sender is expecting acknowledgment packets from the receiver
     
  4. The flow control window advertised by the receiver to the sender is at least $14,600$ bytes

options.label: A
options.text: The congestion window size of the sender is at least $10$ MSS's (or, $14,600$ bytes)

options.label: B
options.text: The congestion window size of the receiver is at least $10$ MSS's (or, $14,600$ bytes)

options.label: C
options.text: The sender is expecting acknowledgment packets from the receiver

options.label: D
options.text: The flow control window advertised by the receiver to the sender is at least $14,600$ bytes

questions.explanation: If $14,600$ bytes are in-flight, the sender's congestion window must be at least $14,600$ bytes. So A is true. The receiver does not have a congestion window at all, it only has a flow-control window, so $B$ is not necessarily true. Since data is outstanding, the sender must be expecting ACKs, so C is true. For the sender to have sent $14,600$ bytes, the receiver's advertised window must be at least $14,600$ bytes, so $D$ is true. questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. By using the port numbers in the TCP header... Explanation: This problem tests your understanding of TCP Demultiplexing. Here is how the Operating System distinguishes between multiple network connections on the same device: IP Address is Insufficient: As stated in the problem, your laptop has only one IP address . All incoming traffic for both the video class and the cat blog arrives at this same destination IP. Therefore, the OS cannot distinguish the packets based on IP alone (ruling out Option A). The Role of Port Numbers: A TCP connection is uniquely identified by a 4-tuple : Source IP Source Port Destination IP Destination Port How it Works: When you open a tab for "GO Classes," your browser assigns a unique, temporary source port (e.g., 5001) to that socket. When you open the "cat blog" tab, it assigns a different source port (e.g., 5002). The Return Path: When the servers send data back to you, they target these specific ports. If a sequence number is chosen uniformly at random from the entire TCP sequence number space ( size $=2^{32}$ ), what is the probability that the sequence number falls inside the advertised window? $\frac{1}{2^{32}}$ $\frac{1}{2^{12}}$ $\frac{1}{2^{20}}$ $\frac{1}{2^{16}}$
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose that the advertised receiver window in TCP is $\mathbf{1}$ Mbyte long. If a sequence number is chosen uniformly at random from the entire TCP sequence number space ( size $=2^{32}$ ), what is the probability that the sequence number falls inside the advertised window?

  1. $\frac{1}{2^{32}}$
     
  2. $\frac{1}{2^{12}}$
     
  3. $\frac{1}{2^{20}}$
     
  4. $\frac{1}{2^{16}}$
questions.explanation: We are given: TCP sequence number space $=2^{32}$. Advertised receiver window size $=1 \mathrm{MB}=2^{20}$. The probability that a random sequence number falls inside the advertised window is: $$ \begin{gathered} P=\frac{\text { Window size }}{\text { Sequence number space }} \\ P=\frac{2^{20}}{2^{32}}=\frac{1}{2^{12}} \end{gathered} $$ GO Classes answered Sep 26, 2025 • edited Sep 26, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply Subh23 commented Nov 29, 2025 reply Follow flag WOW 0 0 reply Share Please log in or register to add a comment. At some point, a TCP connection has the following state:

  • CWND = 4 MSS, SSTHRESH = $8$ MSS
     
  • All packets up to and including $\#411$ have been sent and acknowledged.
     
  • Packets $\#412$ through $\#415$ have been sent but not yet acknowledged.
     
  • Packets $\#416$ and later have not been sent.

Now, assume TCP is in Congestion Avoidance mode.

If an ACK for packet $\#412 $is received, which packet(s) will be sent as a result? (Select all that apply.)

  1. $\#416$
     
  2. $\#417$
     
  3. $\#418$
     
  4. $\#419$
questions.explanation: In Congestion Avoidance, each ACK increases CWND by about $1$/CWND. Here CWND $=4 \mathrm{MSS}$, so after receiving an ACK it becomes $4+1 / 4 \approx 4 \mathrm{MSS}$ (rounded). This allows $4$ packets in flight. Since $\#413, \#414,$ and $\#415$ are already in transit, we can send $\#416$ to keep $4$ packets in flight. questions.questionText: Alice is sending data to Bob over a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection in the congestion avoidance (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease) phase. Maximum Segment Size (MSS) = $100$ bytes Current Congestion Window (CWND) $=1000$ bytes Alice sends a packet with sequence number $801$, and Bob replies with Acknowledgment $(A C K)=901$. What will be the updated Congestion Window (CWND) after this acknowledgement?
questions.questionHtml:
Alice is sending data to Bob over a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection in the congestion avoidance (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease) phase.

  • Maximum Segment Size (MSS) = $100$ bytes
     
  • Current Congestion Window (CWND) $=1000$ bytes
     
  • Alice sends a packet with sequence number $801$, and Bob replies with Acknowledgment $(A C K)=901$.

What will be the updated Congestion Window (CWND) after this acknowledgement?
questions.explanation: In congestion avoidance, the congestion window increases by one MSS ( $100$ bytes) after all $1000$ bytes in the current window are acknowledged. This means: if $1000$ bytes acknowledged $\rightarrow$ CWND increases by $100$ bytes. So, if only $100$ bytes are acknowledged (as in this ACK), the increase is $(100/1000)$ of $100$ bytes $=10$ bytes. Hence, new CWND $= 1000 + 10 = 1010$ bytes. questions.questionText: Consider a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection with the following parameters: Maximum Segment Size (MSS) = $1000$ bytes Initial Congestion Window (CWND) = $1000$ bytes Slow-Start Threshold (SSTHRESH) = $4000$ bytes All data up to byte $6000$ has been acknowledged (so the next expected byte is $6001$ ). Now the sender continues transmitting. After receiving the ACK for the 7th MSS, TCP updates its window. What will be the new CWND ?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection with the following parameters:

  • Maximum Segment Size (MSS) = $1000$ bytes
     
  • Initial Congestion Window (CWND) = $1000$ bytes
     
  • Slow-Start Threshold (SSTHRESH) = $4000$ bytes
     
  • All data up to byte $6000$ has been acknowledged (so the next expected byte is $6001$ ).

Now the sender continues transmitting. After receiving the ACK for the 7th MSS, TCP updates its window.
What will be the new CWND ?
questions.explanation: Initial state: CWND = 1000 bytes (Packet sent $\#1$) After 1st RTT: CWND = 2000 bytes (Packets sent: $\#2, \#3$) After 2nd RTT: CWND = 4000 bytes (Packets sent: $\#4$, $\#5$, $\#6$, $\#7$) Now, the slow start ends because CWND has reached SSTHRESH =$ 4000$. From here, congestion avoidance begins. In congestion avoidance, the rule is: CWND increases by $1$ MSS ($1000$ bytes) when the entire CWND worth of data is acknowledged. That means: On $4000$ bytes acknowledged $\rightarrow$ increment $=1000$ bytes On $1$ byte acknowledged $\rightarrow$ increment $=1000 / 4000=0.25$ bytes On $1000$ bytes acknowledged $($ one MSS $) \rightarrow$ increment $=(1000 / 4000) \times 1000=250$ bytes So, after receiving the ACK for the 7th MSS ($1000$ bytes acknowledged): CWND = $4000 + 250 = 4250$ bytes (Packet sent $\#11$) GO Classes answered Sep 26, 2025 • edited Sep 26, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow See all 2 Comments 2 2 Comments reply i.kshitij commented Oct 28, 2025 reply

questions.questionHtml:
Arrange the steps involved when a user enters a URL in a browser and accesses a website.

  1. DNS resolution
  2. HTTP request sent
  3. URL entered in the browser
  4. IP address obtained
  5. Webpage displayed

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  1. $\text{II, I, III, V, IV}$
  2. $\text{III, II, I, V, IV}$
  3. $\text{II, III, IV, I, V}$
  4. $\text{III, I, IV, II, V}$
questions.explanation: When a user enters a URL in a browser, the following steps occur in this specific order: URL entered in the browser : The process begins with the user manually typing the URL into the browser's address bar and pressing Enter. DNS resolution : The browser needs to find the IP address corresponding to the domain name in the URL (e.g., www.example.com ). It queries a Domain Name System (DNS) server to translate the human-readable domain name into a machine-readable IP address. IP address obtained : Once the DNS query is successful, the browser receives the IP address of the web server that hosts the website. This IP address is essential for establishing a connection. HTTP request sent : The browser uses the obtained IP address to open a connection to the web server and sends a Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) request, asking for the webpage's content. questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following are controlled-access protocols

  1. Reservation
  2. Polling
  3. TDMA
  4. Token Passing
  5. CSMA/CA

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  1. $\text{I}$ and $\text{IV}$ Only
  2. $\text{I, II}$ and $\text{IV}$ Only
  3. $\text{III, IV}$ and $\text{V}$ Only
  4. $\text{I, IV}$ and $\text{V}$ Only
questions.explanation: The controlled-access protocols are Reservation , Polling , and Token Passing . These protocols ensure that a single station has control over the channel at any given time to avoid collisions. CSMA/CA is a random-access protocol, not a controlled-access protocol. Therefore, the correct answer is A, B, and D Only . other additional info: Contention-Based (or Random Access) Protocols : In these protocols, every station has the same right to transmit data. They don't need any coordination from a central authority. If multiple stations try to transmit at the same time, a collision occurs. Examples include ALOHA and Carrier Sense Multiple Access (CSMA) protocols like CSMA/CD (used in Ethernet) and CSMA/CA (used in Wi-Fi).   Controlled-Access Protocols : In this category, stations must ask permission from another station or a central controller before they can transmit.   3. Amplitude Modulation
  4. Hamming code
  5. Bipolar AMI

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  1. $\text{I, III}$ and $t\text{IV}$ Only
  2. $\text{I, II}$ and $\text{IV}$ Only
  3. $\text{III, IV}$ and $\text{V}$ Only

questions.explanation: The examples of data encoding schemes are Non-Return to Zero (NRZ) , Manchester Encoding , and Bipolar AMI . These are all methods for converting digital data into digital signals. Amplitude Modulation is a modulation technique used to encode information onto an analog carrier signal, not a digital data encoding scheme. Hamming code is an error-correcting code, not an encoding scheme for signal transmission. Therefore, the correct answer is 4 (A, B and E Only) .

questions.questionText: Host $A$ (on $\mathrm{TCP/IPv}4$ Networks) send an IP Datagram $D$ to host $B$ (also on $\mathrm{TCP/IPv}4$ network). Assume that no error occured during transmission of $D$ , when $D$ reaches $B$. Which of following header field may differ from that of original datagram $D$? TTL Checksum Fragment offset Source IP Destination IP Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.questionHtml:
Host $A$ (on $\mathrm{TCP/IPv}4$ Networks) send an IP Datagram $D$ to host $B$ (also on $\mathrm{TCP/IPv}4$ network). Assume that no error occured during transmission of $D$ , when $D$ reaches $B$. Which of following header field may differ from that of original datagram $D$?

  1. TTL
  2. Checksum
  3. Fragment offset
  4. Source IP
  5. Destination IP
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation: When an IP datagram is sent across networks, some header fields change while others must remain unchanged . Let's analyze each field: ✅ (A) TTL (Time To Live) TTL decreases by 1 at every router hop , so it will be different. ✔ Will differ ✅ (B) Checksum The IP header checksum is recalculated every time the packet is modified (such as TTL change). ✔ Will differ ❌ (C) Fragment offset Fragment offset changes only if fragmentation occurs . But the question states "Assume that no error occurred during transmission" , not that fragmentation didn’t occur. However, fragmentation does not depend on errors. It depends on MTU mismatch. Since the question says host A and host B are on the same network , fragmentation will not occur . So fragment offset will NOT change. ✘ Will NOT differ ❌ (D) Source IP Source IP never changes during transmission. ✘ Will NOT differ ❌ (E) Destination IP Destination IP never changes. ✘ Will NOT differ ✅ Correct Answer: (A) and (B) Only

questions.explanation: The given function f(p) = (p+11) mod 26 is a Caesar cipher with a forward shift of 11 . That means every plaintext/Original letter is moved 11 steps ahead to form the ciphertext. To get back the original message, we shift each letter 11 steps backward . When we apply this to " DEZA RWZMLW HLCXTYR. ", it becomes: DEZA  → STOP RWZMLW → GLOBAL HLCXTYR → WARMING So, the decrypted/original message is " STOP GLOBAL WARMING. questions.questionText: In older networking references , the first subnet (all-zeros) and last subnet (all-ones) were considered unusable, so the formula for number of subnets was: $2^n$ − 2 (where n = number of subnet bits) But in modern networking, these subnets are allowed to be used, so the formula becomes: $2^n$ Let me be clear I'm not talking about host, I know we exclude 1st and last host from every subnet. From a GATE exam perspective, which convention should we follow? For example: Class B address with subnet mask 255.255.248.0 Default mask: /16 Given mask: /21 Subnet bits: 5 Number of subnets: Without subtraction: $2^5$ = 32 With subtraction: $2^5$ − 2 = 30 If such a question appears in GATE, should we answer 30 or 32?
questions.questionHtml:
In older networking references , the first subnet (all-zeros) and last subnet (all-ones) were considered unusable, so the formula for number of subnets was:

$2^n$ − 2 (where n = number of subnet bits)

But in modern networking, these subnets are allowed to be used, so the formula becomes:

$2^n$

Let me be clear I'm not talking about host, I know we exclude 1st and last host from every subnet.

From a GATE exam perspective, which convention should we follow?

For example:

Class B address with subnet mask 255.255.248.0

Default mask: /16

Given mask: /21

Subnet bits: 5

Number of subnets:

Without subtraction: $2^5$ = 32

With subtraction: $2^5$ − 2 = 30

 

If such a question appears in GATE, should we answer 30 or 32?

questions.questionText: An IP datagram of total length $1000$ bytes, including a $20$-byte IP header, needs to be transmitted over a network with a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of $512$ bytes. The datagram is fragmented accordingly. Fragmentation must ensure that each fragment's payload size (excluding header) is a multiple of $8$ bytes, except possibly the last fragment. What is the Fragment Offset value (in bytes) for the third fragment? $976$ $122$ $508$ $492$
questions.questionHtml:
An IP datagram of total length $1000$ bytes, including a $20$-byte IP header, needs to be transmitted over a network with a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of $512$ bytes. The datagram is fragmented accordingly. Fragmentation must ensure that each fragment's payload size (excluding header) is a multiple of $8$ bytes, except possibly the last fragment.

What is the Fragment Offset value (in bytes) for the third fragment?

  1. $976$
     
  2. $122$
     
  3. $508$
     
  4. $492$
questions.explanation: Payload $=980$ bytes ($1000-20$) First fragment carries $488$ bytes (offset $0$). Second fragment carries next $488$ bytes (offset $488$) Remaining $4$ bytes go in the third fragment $\rightarrow$ offset $=488+488=976$ bytes Note: While the Fragment Offset field in the IP header is expressed in units of $8$ bytes (i.e., $976 / 8=122$), this question explicitly asks for the value in bytes, so the correct answer is $976$.

questions.questionText: An IP datagram arrives at a router with the following header information: $$ \begin{array}{ll} \text{Length of IP header:} &  \quad 20\ \text{bytes} \\ \text{Total length of IP datagram:} & \quad996\ \text{bytes} \\ \text{DF flag:} & \quad 0 \\ \text{MF flag:} & \quad 1 \\ \text{Fragment offset:} & \quad 122 \\ \end{array} $$ The datagram must now be forwarded over a network with an MTU of only $500$ bytes. Use the information in the IP header to infer the minimum total length of the original datagram (before it was fragmented for the first time). $1500$ bytes $1972$ bytes $1496$ bytes $1118$ bytes
questions.questionHtml:
An IP datagram arrives at a router with the following header information:
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Length of IP header:} &  \quad 20\ \text{bytes} \\
\text{Total length of IP datagram:} & \quad996\ \text{bytes} \\
\text{DF flag:} & \quad 0 \\
\text{MF flag:} & \quad 1 \\
\text{Fragment offset:} & \quad 122 \\
\end{array}
$$
The datagram must now be forwarded over a network with an MTU of only $500$ bytes.
Use the information in the IP header to infer the minimum total length of the original datagram (before it was fragmented for the first time).

  1. $1500$ bytes
     
  2. $1972$ bytes
     
  3. $1496$ bytes
     
  4. $1118$ bytes
questions.explanation: Fragment offset $=122 \Rightarrow$ means the payload in this fragment starts at byte $976$ of the original datagram. This fragment carries $976$ bytes of data (since $996$ total - $20$ header = $976$). So, the data in this fragment ends at byte $1951$. Therefore, the original datagram must have had at least $1952$ bytes of data. Adding the IP header of $\mathbf{2 0}$ bytes from the original datagram (not from the fragments), the minimum total length of the original datagram is $\mathbf{1972}$ bytes. Its just telling you payload in this fragment start at 122*8=976 byte of the original datagram. and with122 offset our minimum datagram size =  976 (this one from offset)  +  976(given 996-20=976)  + (header) = 1952 +20

questions.explanation: In an IPv4 fragment, the second row (i.e., bytes 7 and 8 of the IP header) contains a 16-bit field : Flags + Fragment Offset    (13 bits offset, 3 bits flags) This field is provided as two hexadecimal bytes. Packet Flags + Offset Last 13 Bits (Hex) Packet #1 20 48 048 Packet #2 00 90 090 Packet #3 20 00 000 🔷 Packet #1: 20 48 Take last 13 bits → hex = 048 Decimal = 72, so offset = \(72 \times 8 = \boxed{576 \text{ bytes}}\) 🔷 Packet #2: 00 90 Last 13 bits = 090 Decimal = 144, so offset = \(144 \times 8 = \boxed{1152 \text{ bytes}}\) 🔷 Packet #3: 20 00 Last 13 bits = 000 Decimal = 0, so offset = \(0 \times 8 = \boxed{0 \text{ bytes}}\) Hence, the correct reassembly sequence is: \[ \boxed{\text{Packet #3} \rightarrow \text{Packet #1} \rightarrow \text{Packet #2}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \textbf{Option B} \]

Used for fragmentation} & \text{a) 16-bit Identification Field} \\ \text{ii. Indicates presence of options} & \text{b) 4-bit Header Length} \\ \text{iii. Prevents infinite packet looping} & \text{c) 8-bit TTL} \\ \text{iv. Detects corruption of packet payload} & \text{d) 16-bit Checksum} \\ & \text{e) 8-bit Protocol} \\ & \text{f) none-of-the-above} \\ \end{array} $$ $\mathrm{i} \rightarrow \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{ii} \rightarrow \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{iii} \rightarrow \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{iv} \rightarrow \mathrm{d}$ $\mathrm{i} \rightarrow \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{ii} \rightarrow \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{iii} \rightarrow \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{iv} \rightarrow \mathrm{f}$ i $\rightarrow \mathrm{c}$, ii $\rightarrow \mathrm{a}$, iii $\rightarrow \mathrm{e}$, iv $\rightarrow \mathrm{d}$ $\mathrm{i} \rightarrow \mathrm{e}, \mathrm{ii} \rightarrow \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{iii} \rightarrow \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{iv} \rightarrow \mathrm{f}$
questions.questionHtml:
Match the following IP header fields (Column B) to their respective functions (Column A). Use option $\mathbf{f)}$ if none of the given fields apply.
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Column A (Purpose)} & \text{Column B (Field)} \\
\text{i. Used for fragmentation} & \text{a) 16-bit Identification Field} \\
\text{ii. Indicates presence of options} & \text{b) 4-bit Header Length} \\
\text{iii. Prevents infinite packet looping} & \text{c) 8-bit TTL} \\
\text{iv. Detects corruption of packet payload} & \text{d) 16-bit Checksum} \\
& \text{e) 8-bit Protocol} \\
& \text{f) none-of-the-above} \\
\end{array}
$$

  1. $\mathrm{i} \rightarrow \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{ii} \rightarrow \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{iii} \rightarrow \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{iv} \rightarrow \mathrm{d}$
     
  2. $\mathrm{i} \rightarrow \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{ii} \rightarrow \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{iii} \rightarrow \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{iv} \rightarrow \mathrm{f}$
     
  3. i $\rightarrow \mathrm{c}$, ii $\rightarrow \mathrm{a}$, iii $\rightarrow \mathrm{e}$, iv $\rightarrow \mathrm{d}$
     
  4. $\mathrm{i} \rightarrow \mathrm{e}, \mathrm{ii} \rightarrow \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{iii} \rightarrow \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{iv} \rightarrow \mathrm{f}$
questions.explanation: $\mathbf{i} \rightarrow \mathbf{a}$ : The Identification Field is used to uniquely identify fragments of an original IP datagram so they can be reassembled correctly. $\mathbf{i i} \rightarrow \mathbf{b}$ : The Header Length field is 4 bits and indicates the length of the IP header. If it is more than 5 (i.e., more than 20 bytes), options are present. $\mathbf{iii} \rightarrow \mathbf{c}$ : The TTL (Time to Live) field is used to prevent a datagram from circulating indefinitely. Each router decrements it by 1 , and the packet is dropped when TTL reaches 0. $\mathbf{iv} \rightarrow \mathbf{f}$ : The Checksum field only verifies the IP header, not the payload. Therefore, none of the listed fields detect corruption of the payload.

questions.questionText: A computer virus is spreading in a network of $128$ computers. At the beginning (round $0$), only $1$ computer is infected. In each round, every infected computer spreads the virus to $2$ new uninfected computers. The virus is smart and never tries to infect a computer that is already infected. All infections in a round happen at the same time. After that, the next round begins. How many rounds (after the starting point) are needed to infect all $128$ computers?
questions.questionHtml:
A computer virus is spreading in a network of $128$ computers.

  • At the beginning (round $0$), only $1$ computer is infected.
     
  • In each round, every infected computer spreads the virus to $2$ new uninfected computers.
     
  • The virus is smart and never tries to infect a computer that is already infected.
     
  • All infections in a round happen at the same time. After that, the next round begins.

How many rounds (after the starting point) are needed to infect all $128$ computers?
questions.explanation: Let's count how many computers are infected at the end of each round: Round $0$: $1$ computer infected (starting point) Round $1$: $1$ computer infects $2$ new $\rightarrow$ total $=1+2=3$ Round $2$: $3$ computers infect $6$ new $\rightarrow$ total $=3+6=9$ Round $3$: $9$ computers infect $18$ new $\rightarrow$ total $=9+18=27$ Round $4$: $27$ computers infect $54$ new $\rightarrow$ total $=27+54=81$ Round $5$: $81$ computers infect $162$ new $\rightarrow$ total $=81+162=243$ After $5$ rounds (not counting the starting point), all $128$ computers are infected. questions.questionText: We can think of the network as a tree, with the video server at the root and the one million subscribers $\left(10^{6}\right)$ at the leaves. Assuming that the tree has degree four (i.e., each router in the tree connects to four routers closer to the leaves), then roughly how many routers does a packet pass through from the root to each subscriber? $2$ $15$ $10$ $20$
questions.questionHtml:
We can think of the network as a tree, with the video server at the root and the one million subscribers $\left(10^{6}\right)$ at the leaves. Assuming that the tree has degree four (i.e., each router in the tree connects to four routers closer to the leaves), then roughly how many routers does a packet pass through from the root to each subscriber?

  1. $2$
     
  2. $15$
     
  3. $10$
     
  4. $20$
questions.explanation: Let the depth of the tree (i.e., the number of routers a packet passes through from the root to a leaf) be $h$. At each level of the tree, the number of nodes grows as: $$ \text { Number of leaf nodes }=4^{h} $$ We are told: $$ 4^{h} \approx 10^{6} $$ Taking logarithm base 4 on both sides: $$ h=\log _{4}\left(10^{6}\right) $$ Using the change of base formula: $$ h=\frac{\log _{10}\left(10^{6}\right)}{\log _{10}(4)}=\frac{6}{\log _{10}(4)} $$ We know: $$ \log _{10}(4)=\log _{10}\left(2^{2}\right)=2 \cdot \log _{10}(2) \approx 2 \cdot 0.3010=0.602 $$ So: $$ h \approx \frac{6}{0.602} \approx 9.97 \approx 10 $$ Thus, the number of routers a packet passes through from the root to a subscriber is approximately: $10$ GO Classes answered Aug 2, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes 10^6  ~ 2^20 (2^2)^x = 2^20 => (2^2)^x = (2^2)^10 =>   x = 10 suryakumarus answered Nov 22, 2025 suryakumarus comment Share Follow 0

questions.questionText: Consider the following topology, where a node labelled with $\mathbf{N}$ denotes an end system, $\mathbf{H}$ denotes a hub, $\mathbf{S}$ denotes a switch, and $\mathbf{R}$ denotes a router: All links are Ethernet. In an Ethernet-based network, suppose node $N 1$ constructs a packet and accidentally flips a single bit in the IP header before constructing the Ethernet frame; i.e., Ethernet CRC is calculated after the bit flip. Where in the network will this error be detected and the packet dropped? At the hub $H 1$, due to Ethernet CRC failure. At the router $R 1$, due to invalid IP header checksum. At the router $R 2$, due to invalid IP header checksum. At the switch $S 1$, due to Ethernet CRC failure.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following topology, where a node labelled with $\mathbf{N}$ denotes an end system, $\mathbf{H}$ denotes a hub, $\mathbf{S}$ denotes a switch, and $\mathbf{R}$ denotes a router:



All links are Ethernet.
In an Ethernet-based network, suppose node $N 1$ constructs a packet and accidentally flips a single bit in the IP header before constructing the Ethernet frame; i.e., Ethernet CRC is calculated after the bit flip. Where in the network will this error be detected and the packet dropped?

  1. At the hub $H 1$, due to Ethernet CRC failure.
     
  2. At the router $R 1$, due to invalid IP header checksum.
     
  3. At the router $R 2$, due to invalid IP header checksum.
     
  4. At the switch $S 1$, due to Ethernet CRC failure.

options.label: A
options.text: At the hub $H 1$, due to Ethernet CRC failure.

options.label: B
options.text: At the router $R 1$, due to invalid IP header checksum.

options.label: C
options.text: At the router $R 2$, due to invalid IP header checksum.

options.label: D
options.text: At the switch $S 1$, due to Ethernet CRC failure.

questions.explanation: Option A: Incorrect . A hub operates at Layer $1$ (physical layer) and does not inspect or validate CRC. It simply forwards electrical signals to all ports. Option B: Correct. The IP header has its own checksum field. Since the bit flip occurs before Ethernet CRC calculation, the Ethernet frame is valid. However, when router $R 1$ checks the IP header, the IP checksum will not match, and the router will drop the packet. Option C: Incorrect . The error will be detected at router $R 1$ itself, so the packet will never reach $R 2$. Option D: Incorrect . The Ethernet CRC was calculated after the bit flip, so the frame appears valid at the data link layer. Moreover, switches do not inspect IP headers; they only forward based on MAC addresses.

questions.questionHtml:
In a Go-Back-N (GBN) protocol, the sender uses a window size of $4$ and sequence numbers range from $0$ to $1023$ (modulo $1024$). Suppose the sender had transmitted packets with sequence numbers $500,501,502$, and $503$ , and $500$ was the base of the sender's window. After a while, the sender receives an ACK for packet $500$.

Assume:

  • The ACK is cumulative.
  • No other ACKs have been received.
  • No timeouts have occurred yet.


Which of the following statements is/are correct?
 

  1. The sender can now send packet $504$ immediately.
  2. The sender must retransmit packet $500$, since no ACK for $501$ has been received.
  3. The new sender window is [$501, 504$], and packets $501-503$ can be retransmitted if timeout occurs.
  4. The base of the sender window remains unchanged until ACKs for all packets $500-503$ are received.

options.label: A
options.text: The sender can now send packet $504$ immediately.

options.label: B
options.text: The sender must retransmit packet $500$, since no ACK for $501$ has been received.

options.label: C
options.text: The new sender window is [$501, 504$], and packets $501-503$ can be retransmitted if timeout occurs.

options.label: D
options.text: The base of the sender window remains unchanged until ACKs for all packets $500-503$ are received.

questions.explanation: What happens after ACK(500)? -------------------------------- - New base = 501 - New window = [501, 502, 503, 504] - Outstanding packets = 501, 502, 503 (not yet acked) - One slot is free → sender * can * send 504 immediately - ✅ This makes Option (1) true. Timeout behavior in GBN -------------------------------- - Timeout is always tied to the oldest unacked packet (the base). - When base times out, **all outstanding packets (sent but unacked) starting from base** are retransmitted. - Current base = 501 → if 501’s timer expires, retransmission starts from 501 onward. Two cases for packet 504 -------------------------------- 1. **504 is sent before timeout occurs**           - Outstanding = {501, 502, 503, 504}           - On timeout of 501 → retransmit {501, 502, 503, 504} 2. **504 is not sent before timeout occurs**            - Outstanding = {501, 502, 503}            - On

questions.questionHtml:
A sender using the Go-Back-N protocol has a current window of size $4$ , which includes the sequence numbers $100,101,102$, and $103$ . The sender has sent packets $100$ and $101$ so far.

Which of the following statements must be true?
 

  1. Packet $100$ has been sent and acknowledged.
  2. Packet $103$ is outside the window and cannot be sent yet.
  3. If packet $102$ is sent, then packet $101$ must have already been sent.
  4. If packet $102$ has not been sent, then packet $101$ must not have been sent either.

options.label: A
options.text: Packet $100$ has been sent and acknowledged.

options.label: B
options.text: Packet $103$ is outside the window and cannot be sent yet.

options.label: C
options.text: If packet $102$ is sent, then packet $101$ must have already been sent.

options.label: D
options.text: If packet $102$ has not been sent, then packet $101$ must not have been sent either.

questions.explanation: Explanation: Go-Back-N requires that packets be sent in-order. So if packet $102$ is sent, all earlier packets ($100$ and $101$) must have been sent before it. However, the reverse is not necessarily true-just because $102$ is not sent doesn't mean $101$ wasn't sent. Option A: False. If $p_{k}$ were acknowledged, the sender's window would have moved forward. Since $p_{k}$ is still the first packet in the window, it means it has been sent but not yet acknowledged. Option B: False. $p_{k+3}$ is within the sender's window, so it is usable. However, the statement "not sent" is not necessarily true - the sender may or may not have sent it. So this option does not must be true. Option C: True. In Go-Back-N, packets are sent in order. Therefore, if $p_{k+2}$ is sent, it implies that $p_{k+1}$ must have already been sent. Option D: False. Even if $p_{k+2}$ has not been sent, it is still possible that $p_{k+1}$ has been sent. There is no strict dependency in this direction. GO Classes answered

questions.questionText: Node A wants to send a large amount of data to Node C via an intermediate Node B using the Selective Repeat protocol . Each bit transmitted on link $A-B$ has a probability $p$ of getting corrupted Each bit transmitted on link B-C has a probability $q$ of getting corrupted Bit errors occur independently across links and across bits Each data packet is $d$ bits long, and each ACK is $a$ bits long. The ACK is sent end-to-end from C to A (via B $\rightarrow A$ ) What is the expected number of transmissions required by A to successfully send one packet and get it acknowledged? $1 / X$, where $X=(1-p)^{d}(1-q)^{d}(1-q)^{a}(1-p)^{a}$ $1 / X$, where $X=(1-p)^{d}(1-q)^{a}$ $1 / X$, where $X=(1-p)^{d}(1-q)^{d}(1-p)^{a}$ $1 / X$, where $X=(1-p)^{d}(1-q)^{d}(1-q)^{a}$
questions.questionHtml:
Node A wants to send a large amount of data to Node C via an intermediate Node B using the Selective Repeat protocol .

  • Each bit transmitted on link $A-B$ has a probability $p$ of getting corrupted
  • Each bit transmitted on link B-C has a probability $q$ of getting corrupted
  • Bit errors occur independently across links and across bits


Each data packet is $d$ bits long, and each ACK is $a$ bits long. The ACK is sent end-to-end from C to A (via B $\rightarrow A$ )

What is the expected number of transmissions required by A to successfully send one packet and get it acknowledged?
 

  1. $1 / X$, where $X=(1-p)^{d}(1-q)^{d}(1-q)^{a}(1-p)^{a}$
  2. $1 / X$, where $X=(1-p)^{d}(1-q)^{a}$
  3. $1 / X$, where $X=(1-p)^{d}(1-q)^{d}(1-p)^{a}$
  4. $1 / X$, where $X=(1-p)^{d}(1-q)^{d}(1-q)^{a}$
questions.explanation: Probability that the packet is transmitted from A to B without error: $$ P_{\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{~B}}=(1-p)^{d} $$ Probability that the packet is transmitted from B to C without error: $$ P_{\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}}=(1-q)^{d} $$ The ACK travels from C to A via B: $$ P_{\mathrm{ACK}}=(1-q)^{a} \cdot(1-p)^{a} $$ Total Success Probability $$ X=(1-p)^{d}(1-q)^{d}(1-q)^{a}(1-p)^{a} $$ Expected Number of Transmissions $$ E[\text { transmissions }]=\frac{1}{X}=\frac{1}{(1-p)^{d}(1-q)^{d}(1-q)^{a}(1-p)^{a}} $$ GO Classes answered Jul 30, 2025 • edited Jul 30, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: In a sliding window protocol, the sender and receiver both use a window size of $N=5$. The sequence number space ranges from $0$ to $15$ . At a certain time, the sender's window includes the sequence numbers $0$ to $4$ , and the receiver's window includes the sequence numbers $2$ to $6$ . Which of the following best describes the current state? The sender has received ACKs for packets $0$ and $1$ , and has sent packets $2$ to $4$. The receiver is expecting packet $0$ , as it has not received any packets yet. The sender has sent packets $0$ to $4$ , and packets $0$ and $1$ have been acknowledged. The receiver has received packets $0$ to $2$ , and is waiting for $3$ to $7$ .
questions.questionHtml:
In a sliding window protocol, the sender and receiver both use a window size of $N=5$. The sequence number space ranges from $0$ to $15$ . At a certain time, the sender's window includes the sequence numbers $0$ to $4$ , and the receiver's window includes the sequence numbers $2$ to $6$ . Which of the following best describes the current state?
 

  1. The sender has received ACKs for packets $0$ and $1$ , and has sent packets $2$ to $4$.
     
  2. The receiver is expecting packet $0$ , as it has not received any packets yet.
     
  3. The sender has sent packets $0$ to $4$ , and packets $0$ and $1$ have been acknowledged.
     
  4. The receiver has received packets $0$ to $2$ , and is waiting for $3$ to $7$ .

options.label: A
options.text: The sender has received ACKs for packets $0$ and $1$ , and has sent packets $2$ to $4$.

options.label: B
options.text: The receiver is expecting packet $0$ , as it has not received any packets yet.

options.label: C
options.text: The sender has sent packets $0$ to $4$ , and packets $0$ and $1$ have been acknowledged.

options.label: D
options.text: The receiver has received packets $0$ to $2$ , and is waiting for $3$ to $7$ .

questions.explanation: The sender’s window is \([0,1,2,3,4]\). This means packets \(0\) and \(1\) have already been acknowledged, otherwise the sender’s window would have started earlier. Hence, the sender has sent packets \(0\) to \(4\), and ACKs for \(0\) and \(1\) are received.   The receiver’s window is \([2,3,4,5,6]\). This indicates that it has already received packets \(0\) and \(1\), and is now expecting packet \(2\) as the next in-order packet.   Thus, the correct description is that the sender has sent packets \(0\) to \(4\), and packets \(0\) and \(1\) have been acknowledged.   \[ \boxed{\text{Option C}} \]

questions.questionHtml:
Suppose it takes $1$ ms to send a packet, and the one-way propagation delay between the sender and receiver is $\mathbf{1 0} \mathbf{~ m s}$. The sliding window size is again $N=4$. What is the channel (or link) utilization?

  1. $19.05 \%$
     
  2. $25 \%$
     
  3. $33.3 \%$
     
  4. $40 \%$
questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. 19.05% Explanation: Transmission time per packet $=1 \mathrm{~ms}$ One-way propagation delay $=10 \mathrm{~ms}$ Round-trip time $(\mathrm{RTT})=2 \times 10=20 \mathrm{~ms}$ Sliding window size $N=4$ Channel utilization $U$ is given by: $$ U=\frac{N \times \text { Transmission Time }}{\text { RTT }+ \text { Transmission Time }}=\frac{4 \times 1}{20+1}=\frac{4}{21} \approx 0.1905=19.05 \% $$

  • One-way link latency $=10 \mathrm{~ms}$

When is packet $3$ first retransmitted (i.e., sent again after timeout expiry)?

  3. $t=103 \mathrm{~ms}$
  4. $t=100 \mathrm{~ms}$
questions.explanation: Explanation: At $t=0$, sender starts transmitting: Packet Sent at (ms) 0 0 1 1 2 2 3 3 (Lost) 4 4 Receiver side: Packet $0$ reaches at $0+10=10 \mathrm{~ms} \rightarrow \mathrm{ACK}$ at $20$ ms Packet $1 \rightarrow \mathrm{ACK}$ at $21$ ms Packet $2 \rightarrow \mathrm{ACK}$ at $22$ ms Packet $3$ is lost $\Rightarrow$ No ACK beyond packet $2$ is sent Sender view: ACKs for packets $0,1,2$ received by $t=22 \mathrm{~ms}$ No ACK for packet $3$ or beyond Timeout: Timeout for packet 3 starts at $t=3 \mathrm{~ms}$ Timeout expires at $3+100=103 \mathrm{~ms}$ At $t=103 \mathrm{~ms}$, the sender retransmits packet $3$. Since this is Go-Back-N, it will go back and retransmit packet $3$ and subsequent packets as needed. questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following fields in IPv 4 datagram is not related to fragmentation?

  1. Type of service
  2. Fragment offset
  3. Flags
  4. Indentification
questions.explanation: Answer: Option A)  Type of service.  In IPv4 datagrams, fragmentation is the process of breaking a large packet into smaller pieces to fit the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of the network. The fields related to fragmentation are: Fragment Offset : Indicates the position of the fragment in the original datagram. Flags : Includes bits like "More Fragments" and "Don't Fragment" which control fragmentation behavior. Identification : Used to uniquely identify fragments of the original datagram so they can be reassembled correctly. 🔹 Type of Service (ToS) ,  is used for specifying the priority and handling of the packet (like delay, throughput, reliability), and is not related to fragmentation .

questions.questionText: A $4$-bit message is encoded using the ($7$,$4$) Hamming code   (4 data bits + 3 parity bits)   and transmitted over a noisy communication channel. The received $7$-bit message is: Received codeword: $0010011$ The bits are arranged as follows (from left to right): $$ \text{x}_{7} \ \text{x}_{6} \ \text{x}_{5} \ \text{x}_{4} \ \text{x}_{3} \ \text{x}_{2} \ \text{x}_{1} = d_{3} \ d_{2} \ d_{1} \ p_{4} \ d_{0} \ p_{2} \ p_{1} $$ All parity bits use even parity. The parity conditions are: $$ \begin{aligned} & p_{1}: \text{x}_{7} \oplus \text{x}_{5} \oplus \text{x}_{3} \oplus \text{x}_{1} = 0 \\ & p_{2}: \text{x}_{7} \oplus \text{x}_{6} \oplus \text{x}_{3} \oplus \text{x}_{2} = 0 \\ & p_{4}: \text{x}_{7} \oplus \text{x}_{6} \oplus \text{x}_{5} \oplus \text{x}_{4} = 0 \end{aligned} $$ Is there a single-bit error in the received codeword? If yes, which bit is incorrect, and what was the original $4$-bit message? No error; original $4$-bit message is $0010$ Error in bit position $1$; original $4$-bit message is $0010$ Error in bit position $4$; original $4$-bit message is $0110$ Error in bit position $5$; original $4$-bit message is $0011$
questions.questionHtml:
A $4$-bit message is encoded using the ($7$,$4$) Hamming code  (4 data bits + 3 parity bits) and transmitted over a noisy communication channel. The received $7$-bit message is:

Received codeword: $0010011$

The bits are arranged as follows (from left to right):
$$ \text{x}_{7} \ \text{x}_{6} \ \text{x}_{5} \ \text{x}_{4} \ \text{x}_{3} \ \text{x}_{2} \ \text{x}_{1} = d_{3} \ d_{2} \ d_{1} \ p_{4} \ d_{0} \ p_{2} \ p_{1} $$

All parity bits use even parity. The parity conditions are:
$$ \begin{aligned} & p_{1}: \text{x}_{7} \oplus \text{x}_{5} \oplus \text{x}_{3} \oplus \text{x}_{1} = 0 \\ & p_{2}: \text{x}_{7} \oplus \text{x}_{6} \oplus \text{x}_{3} \oplus \text{x}_{2} = 0 \\ & p_{4}: \text{x}_{7} \oplus \text{x}_{6} \oplus \text{x}_{5} \oplus \text{x}_{4} = 0 \end{aligned} $$

Is there a single-bit error in the received codeword? If yes, which bit is incorrect, and what was the original $4$-bit message?

  1. No error; original $4$-bit message is $0010$
     
  2. Error in bit position $1$; original $4$-bit message is $0010$
     
  3. Error in bit position $4$; original $4$-bit message is $0110$
     
  4. Error in bit position $5$; original $4$-bit message is $0011$

options.label: B
options.text: Error in bit position $1$; original $4$-bit message is $0010$

options.label: C
options.text: Error in bit position $4$; original $4$-bit message is $0110$

options.label: D
options.text: Error in bit position $5$; original $4$-bit message is $0011$

questions.explanation: Received bits: $\text{x}_{7} \ \text{x}_{6} \ \text{x}_{5} \ \text{x}_{4} \ \text{x}_{3} \ \text{x}_{2} \ \text{x}_{1} = 0010011$ We now compute the parity check values using even parity conditions: $$ \begin{aligned} & E_{1} = \text{x}_{7} \oplus \text{x}_{5} \oplus \text{x}_{3} \oplus \text{x}_{1} = 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 = 0 \\ & E_{2} = \text{x}_{7} \oplus \text{x}_{6} \oplus \text{x}_{3} \oplus \text{x}_{2} = 0 \oplus 0 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 = 1 \\ & E_{4} = \text{x}_{7} \oplus \text{x}_{6} \oplus \text{x}_{5} \oplus \text{x}_{4} = 0 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 = 1 \end{aligned} $$ The syndrome is formed by concatenating the parity results in the order $E_{4} E_{2} E_{1}$, which gives $110_2 = 6$. This indicates that the error is in bit position $6$ (counting from the right, starting at position $1$). Flipping bit $6$ in the received codeword $0010011$ gives the corrected codeword: $0011011$.

questions.explanation: g(x) is divisible by x+1 as putting 1 gives g(1)=0. So g(x) can be written as (x+1).f(x).  OPTION A:  A single bit error can never be divided as x^0 is present so as it can never be divided , it can be detected always. OPTION B: 2 bit error can be written as x^i + x^j this error is divisible by x+1 therefore can be written as (x+1)p(x) . so we can design the error such that p(x) is not divisible by f(x) hence we can say some 2 bit errors can be detected. OPTION C :  Any error with odd number of bits cannot be factorised into (x+1)(something) , hence (x+1).f(x) will never be able to divide the error hence all error with odd numbers of bits are detected. questions.explanation: Problem: Analyze the error detection ability of $G(x) = 1101111$. Analysis: The polynomial corresponds to $x^6 + x^5 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1$. A key property of generator polynomials involves the factor $(x+1)$. If $(x+1)$ is a factor of $G(x)$, the code can detect all errors with an odd number of bit flips. We can test this by substituting $x=1$ into the polynomial (using modulo-2 arithmetic): $$G(1) = 1^6 + 1^5 + 1^3 + 1^2 + 1 + 1$$ $$G(1) = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 \equiv 0 \pmod 2$$ Since $G(1) = 0$, the polynomial is divisible by $(x+1)$. Conclusion: This generator guarantees the detection of all odd-numbered bit errors. Answer: D. questions.questionText: A block code uses 3 data bits \(D_1, D_2, D_3\) and 3 parity bits \(P_1, P_2, P_3\), resulting in a 6-bit codeword. The parity bits are calculated at the sender using equations shown in Table A . At the receiver, three error indicators \(E_1, E_2, E_3\) are computed as shown in Table B . Table A: Parity Bit Equations $$ \begin{array}{|l|} \hline P_1 = D_1 + D_2 \\ P_2 = D_2 + D_3 \\ P_3 = D_3 + D_1 \\ \hline \end{array} $$
questions.questionHtml:
A block code uses 3 data bits \(D_1, D_2, D_3\) and 3 parity bits \(P_1, P_2, P_3\), resulting in a 6-bit codeword. The parity bits are calculated at the sender using equations shown in Table A. At the receiver, three error indicators \(E_1, E_2, E_3\) are computed as shown in Table B.

Table A:
Parity Bit Equations

$$ \begin{array}{|l|} \hline P_1 = D_1 + D_2 \\ P_2 = D_2 + D_3 \\ P_3 = D_3 + D_1 \\ \hline \end{array} $$
questions.explanation: The received error indicator pattern is: $$ E_1 = 0, \quad E_2 = 1, \quad E_3 = 0 $$ Only the second parity check equation has failed. Let's analyze what this tells us. From Table B: $$ E_2 = D_2 + D_3 + P_2 $$ If there had been an error in a data bit like \( D_2 \) or \( D_3 \), then it would have affected multiple error equations, because: \( D_2 \) appears in both \( E_1 \) and \( E_2 \) \( D_3 \) appears in both \( E_2 \) and \( E_3 \) But since both \( E_1 \) and \( E_3 \) are zero, it means \( D_2 \) and \( D_3 \) are likely correct. The only remaining bit that appears only in \( E_2 \) is the parity bit \( P_2 \). So, the most likely conclusion is that a single-bit error occurred in parity bit \( P_2 \). Correct answer: C. A single-bit error occurred in parity bit \( P_2 \)

When $E(x)$ has a degree less than that of $G(x)$ When $G(x)$ has degree less than $C(x)$ When the error polynomial $E(x)$ is divisible by the generator polynomial $G(x)$ When the received polynomial $R(x)$ is divisible by the generator polynomial $G(x)$
questions.questionHtml:
In a communication system using CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check), the following notations are used:

  • $C(x)$ : the codeword polynomial transmitted by the sender
     
  • $R(x)$ : the polynomial received by the receiver
     
  • $G(x)$ : the generator polynomial
     
  • $E(x)$ : the error pattern polynomial


Under which of the following conditions can an error go undetected?
 

  1. When $E(x)$ has a degree less than that of $G(x)$
  2. When $G(x)$ has degree less than $C(x)$
  3. When the error polynomial $E(x)$ is divisible by the generator polynomial $G(x)$
  4. When the received polynomial $R(x)$ is divisible by the generator polynomial $G(x)$

options.label: A
options.text: When $E(x)$ has a degree less than that of $G(x)$

options.label: C
options.text: When the error polynomial $E(x)$ is divisible by the generator polynomial $G(x)$

options.label: D
options.text: When the received polynomial $R(x)$ is divisible by the generator polynomial $G(x)$

questions.explanation: An error is undetected if the error polynomial $E(x)$ is divisible by the generator polynomial $G(x)$. In that case, the received polynomial $R(x)=C(x)+E(x)$ is also divisible by $G(x)$, and the CRC check gives zero remainder - making the error invisible to the receiver. GO Classes answered Jul 10, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 1 1 vote We need subnets that support at least 25 usable hosts and minimise wasted addresses. For a prefix /m, usable hosts = 2^(32−m) − 2 A. /25 → 2^7 − 2 = 126 (meets requirement, but wastes many addresses.) B. /26 → 2^6 − 2 = 62 (meets requirement, still has excess.) C. /27 → 2^5 − 2 = 30 ✔︎ (meets requirement and is smaller (less waste) than /26 or /25.) D. /28 → 2^4 − 2 = 14 (does not meet the 25-host requirement.) Thus the smallest mask that gives ≥25 usable hosts is /27 (255.255.255.224) . Assume an organisation is assigned the IP address block $140.25.0.0/16$. The organisation decides to subnet this block using a $/27$ mask.
What is the maximum number of such $/27$ subnets that can be formed from the original address block?

  1. $256$
  2. $512$
  3. $8192$
  4. $2048$

questions.questionText: An organisation has been allocated the IP block $10.0.0.0/24$ to set up a subnet LAN1 that must support 40 hosts, including space for a network address, a broadcast address, and one router interface. Two subnetting strategies are considered: Method 1: Use a single subnet of size /26, which allocates 64 IP addresses. Method 2: Split LAN1 into two smaller subnets : one subnet with 32 addresses (/27) and one subnet with 16 addresses (/28) Which of the following statements is correct regarding address utilisation? Method 1 is more efficient because it uses a single continuous block of 64 addresses. Method 2 is invalid since subnets of this size $/ 27$ and $/ 28$ cannot coexist in the same /24 block. Both methods are equally efficient since both satisfy the 40-host requirement. Method 2 is more efficient, as it allocates only $32+16=48$ addresses instead of 64.
questions.questionHtml:
An organisation has been allocated the IP block $10.0.0.0/24$ to set up a subnet LAN1 that must support 40 hosts, including space for a network address, a broadcast address, and one router interface.
Two subnetting strategies are considered:

  • Method 1: Use a single subnet of size /26, which allocates 64 IP addresses.
  • Method 2: Split LAN1 into two smaller subnets: one subnet with 32 addresses (/27) and one subnet with 16 addresses (/28)

Which of the following statements is correct regarding address utilisation?

  1. Method 1 is more efficient because it uses a single continuous block of 64 addresses.
     
  2. Method 2 is invalid since subnets of this size $/ 27$ and $/ 28$ cannot coexist in the same /24 block.
     
  3. Both methods are equally efficient since both satisfy the 40-host requirement.
     
  4. Method 2 is more efficient, as it allocates only $32+16=48$ addresses instead of 64.

options.label: A
options.text: Method 1 is more efficient because it uses a single continuous block of 64 addresses.

options.label: B
options.text: Method 2 is invalid since subnets of this size $/ 27$ and $/ 28$ cannot coexist in the same /24 block.

options.label: C
options.text: Both methods are equally efficient since both satisfy the 40-host requirement.

options.label: D
options.text: Method 2 is more efficient, as it allocates only $32+16=48$ addresses instead of 64.

questions.explanation: Method 1: Uses a /26 subnet $$ 2^{6}=64 \text { addresses allocated } $$ Method 2: Uses a /27 and a /28 subnet $$ 2^{5}+2^{4}=32+16=48 \text { addresses allocated } $$ Since both methods provide sufficient usable hosts, Method 2 is clearly more efficient in terms of address utilisation, as it minimizes unused IPs. GO Classes answered Jul 10, 2025 • edited Jul 10, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 1 1 vote Question Analysis: Requirement: Support 40 hosts, plus 1 network address, 1 broadcast address, and 1 router interface. Total IPs needed $\approx 40 \text{ (hosts)} + 3 \text{ (overhead)} = 43$. Method 1: Use a single subnet of size /26 . A /26 block has $2^{(32-26)} = 2^6 = \mathbf{64}$ addresses. This is sufficient to hold 43 IPs. Allocated size: 64 addresses. Method 2: Split LAN1 into two subnets: one of size /27 and one of size /28 . A /27 block has $2^5 = 32$ addresses. A /28 block has $2^4 = 16$ addresses.

questions.questionText: C11. Consider that node $X$ is sending packets to node $Y$. The path from $X$ to $Y$ has a bandwidth of $B_{X Y}=5000$ bytes/second and a propagation delay of $P_{X Y}=100$ milliseconds. The reverse path from $Y$ to $X$ has a bandwidth of $B_{Y X}=9500$ bytes/second and a propagation delay of $P_{Y X}=40$ milliseconds. Suppose the size of the data packets is $S_{D}=500$ bytes and the size of the acknowledgement packets is $S_{A}=95$ bytes. Ignore the size of the header in data packets. Moreover, assume that no data packets or acknowledgement packets are lost during transit and there is no queuing delay. (a) Compute the throughput in bytes/second that the node $X$ can achieve in transmitting to node $Y$ using Stop-and-Wait protocol. (b) Suppose instead of Stop-and-Wait, node $X$ uses Sliding Window protocol. (i) Compute the size of the window $W$, in terms of number of data packets, that node $X$ must use in order to transfer its data at the maximum possible rate. Determine the actual rate $T_{\text {max }}$ that $X$ achieves while utilizing the window of size $W$. (ii) If the bandwidth $B_{Y X}$ of the path from $Y$ to $X$ drops to 125 bytes/second, keeping $B_{X Y}, P_{X Y}, P_{Y X}, S_{D}$ and $S_{A}$ unchanged, can $X$ still achieve the transfer rate $T_{\text {max }}$ ? If so, what is the new window size $W$ ? If not, what is the new limit on $T_{\max }$ that $X$ can achieve?

questions.title: Distance-Vector Routing Algorithm Doubt
questions.excerpt: Distance-Vector Routing Algorithm written in FOROUZAN:Distance_Vector_Routing ( ) { // Initialize (create initial vectors for the node) D[myself] = 0 for (y = 1 to N) { i...
questions.questionText: Distance-Vector Routing Algorithm written in FOROUZAN: Distance_Vector_Routing ( ) { // Initialize (create initial vectors for the node) D[myself] = 0 for (y = 1 to N) { if (y is a neighbor) D[y] = c[myself][y] else D[y] = ∞ } send vector {D[1], D[2], ..., D[N]} to all neighbors // Update (improve the vector with the vector received from a neighbor) repeat (forever) { wait (for a vector D_w from a neighbor w or any change in the link) for (y = 1 to N) { D[y] = min(D[y], (c[myself][w] + D_w[y])) // Bellman-Ford equation } if (any change in the vector) send vector {D[1], D[2], ..., D[N]} to all neighbors } } // End of Distance Vector Also about "Two-Node Loop" My Question: Why does node B later accept a higher cost to reach X (e.g., from 2 to 4), even though it initially had a smaller value (2)? Shouldn't it ignore routes that are longer according to the equation  $D[y] = min(D[y], (c[myself][w] + D_w[y]))$?
questions.questionHtml:
Distance-Vector Routing Algorithm written in FOROUZAN:

Distance_Vector_Routing ( )
{
    // Initialize (create initial vectors for the node)
    D[myself] = 0

    for (y = 1 to N)
    {
        if (y is a neighbor)
            D[y] = c[myself][y]
        else
            D[y] = ∞
    }

    send vector {D[1], D[2], ..., D[N]} to all neighbors

    // Update (improve the vector with the vector received from a neighbor)
    repeat (forever)
    {
        wait (for a vector D_w from a neighbor w or any change in the link)

        for (y = 1 to N)
        {
            D[y] = min(D[y], (c[myself][w] + D_w[y]))    // Bellman-Ford equation
        }

        if (any change in the vector)
            send vector {D[1], D[2], ..., D[N]} to all neighbors
    }
} // End of Distance Vector

Also about "Two-Node Loop"

My Question:

Why does node B later accept a higher cost to reach X (e.g., from 2 to 4), even though it initially had a smaller value (2)? Shouldn't it ignore routes that are longer according to the equation $D[y] = min(D[y], (c[myself][w] + D_w[y]))$?

questions.explanation: In Slotted ALOHA , the G represents the average of packets produced by the system . When I say system , I mean to say all the stations are considered as a system . In Slotted ALOHA, we transmit at specific slots (or time frames ). We calculate G for the entire system , not for each station, where G is the number of packets produced in one transmission time by the entire system . So I think the question is not correct, as the question is considering the G for the stations , but it should be for the whole system , or it must have provided some information about how many packets the stations are transmitting .

questions.questionHtml:
Consider a three-link configuration $\text{A-X-Y-B}$, where host $A$ is connected to router $X$, router $X$ is connected to router $Y$, and router $Y$ is connected to host $B$. All nodes support IPv4.

  •   The link $A-X$ has MTU $=1500$ bytes
  •   The link $X-Y$ has MTU $=500$ bytes
  •   The link $Y-B$ has MTU $=492$ bytes

Suppose host $A$ is sending a $1000$-byte packet to host $B$. Assume there is no packet loss due to bit errors or buffer overflow.

Also, assume that the IP header size $=20$ bytes.

How many packets will flow over the $X-Y$ link? And how many will arrive at host $B?$

  1. $3$ packets over $\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{Y}, 5$ packets arrive at host $B.$
  2. $2$ packets over $\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{Y}, 4$ packets arrive at host $B.$
  3. $5$ packets over $\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{Y}, 5$ packets arrive at host $B.$
  4. $3$ packets over $X-Y, 4$ packets arrive at host $B$.

questions.explanation: Please watch this video to solve this question efficiently and clearly. Direct TimeStamp of Detailed Video Solution 3 and 5. The 1000 byte packet from A can go to $X$ without problems, as the MTU on that link is larger than 1000. X has to fragment the packet into fragments of at most 500 bytes each. Since each fragment gets its own 20-byte IP header, the 1000 bytes from A do not fit in two 500-byte fragments, but need three, of sizes 500,500 , and 40 bytes. Each of these fragments arrive at $Y$, which cannot send the 500-byte fragments over the 492 byte MTU of the next link. So those fragments are fragmented further, leading to a total of five fragments arriving at Y. questions.questionHtml:
​​​​​Consider the following statements:

  1. Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address.
  2. A single TCP segment from a sender $S$ to a receiver $R$ cannot carry both data from $S$ to $R$ and acknowledgement for a segment from $R$ to $S$
Which one of the following is CORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address.

options.label: B
options.text: A single TCP segment from a sender $S$ to a receiver $R$ cannot carry both data from $S$ to $R$ and acknowledgement for a segment from $R$ to $S$

questions.explanation: Statement $1$: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address. Explanation: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps an IP address to a MAC address. When a host needs a MAC address for an IP, it sends a broadcast ARP request. The host with the matching IP responds with a unicast ARP reply containing its MAC address. So, Statement $\mathbf{1}$ is true. Statement $2$: A single TCP segment from a sender S to a receiver R cannot carry both data from S to R and acknowledgment for a segment from R to S. Explanation: A single TCP segment from S to R can carry both data and an acknowledgment (ACK) for a previously sent segment from R to S. This type of acknowledgment is known as a piggybacked ACK, where the ACK is included in the same segment that carries the data. So, Statement $\mathbf{2}$ is false. Answer: $\mathbf{(B)}$ benzene06 answered Feb 27, 2025 benzene06 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or regi

questions.explanation: It is given in the question that, Frame size $=L=3000$ bits Transmission rate $= BW = 2000$ bits$/$second   Transmission time for packet $= T_{t} = \dfrac{L}{BW} = \dfrac{3000 \;b}{2000\;b/s} = 1.5 \;sec$ Propogation time $= T_{p} = 100 \;ms = 0.1 \;sec$ Channel Utilization for Stop $\&$ Wait Protocol $= \dfrac{T_{t}}{T_{t}\;+\;2T_{p}}$ $= \dfrac{1.5}{1.5\;+\;2\times0.1}$ $= \dfrac{1.5}{1.7}$ $= 0.8823$ Channel Utilization in percentage $\mathbf{=88.23\;\%}$ Answer: $(A)$ benzene06 answered Feb 27, 2025 • edited Mar 27, 2025 by benzene06 benzene06 comment Share Follow See all 2 Comments 2 2 Comments reply Vansh462 commented Jan 31 reply Follow flag 'size of acknowledgement is negligible' we won't consider p_ack also negligible Making 1.5/1.6 = 0.9375 As p_ack is always = p_time so your answer is right 1.5/1.7 = 0.8823 ✅ 1 1 reply Share Randy_Rushendran commented Feb 11 reply Follow flag Hey started studing CN today, can you justify your answer? like y

A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 7488 bytes.  Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including IPv4 header? 5 fragments, 1488 bytes 6 fragments, 88 bytes 6 fragments, 108 bytes 6 fragments, 116 bytes
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of 1500 bytes in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 7488 bytes. 

Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including IPv4 header?

  1. 5 fragments, 1488 bytes
  2. 6 fragments, 88 bytes
  3. 6 fragments, 108 bytes
  4. 6 fragments, 116 bytes
questions.explanation: MTU $= 1500$ B It is given that IPv4 headers do not use any options field, that means IPv4 Header Size is $20$ B. IP Header Size $= 20$ B So, MTU without IP Header $= (1500 - 20)$ Bytes $= 1480 $ Bytes Now, Payload for UDP Segment is $7488$ Bytes. UDP Header is of $8$ Bytes. So,  Payload for IP datagram $=$ Payload for UDP segment $+$ UDP Header. $= 7488 + 8 = 7496$ Now, fragmenting this Payload for IP Datagram using MTU without IP Header. Total Fragments $= 6$ Last packet data without header $= 96$ Bytes Last packet size with IP Header $= 96 + 20 = 116$ Bytes. So, Total no of fragments are $\mathbf{6}$ and size of last packet including IP Header is $\mathbf{116}$ Bytes. Answer: $\mathbf{D}$ benzene06 answered Feb 27, 2025 benzene06 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 1 1 vote Answer : D Vamsi bankupalli answered May 27, 2025 Vamsi bankupalli comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Consider the following statements: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address. A single TCP segment from a sender S to a receiver R cannot carry both data from S to R and acknowledgment for a segment from R to S. Which ONE of the following is CORRECT? Both (i) and (ii) are TRUE (i) is TRUE and (ii) is FALSE (i) is FALSE and (ii) is TRUE Both (i) and (ii) are FALSE
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following statements:

  1. Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address.
  2. A single TCP segment from a sender S to a receiver R cannot carry both data from S to R and acknowledgment for a segment from R to S.

Which ONE of the following is CORRECT?

 

  1. Both (i) and (ii) are TRUE
  2. (i) is TRUE and (ii) is FALSE
  3. (i) is FALSE and (ii) is TRUE
  4. Both (i) and (ii) are FALSE
questions.explanation: Statement $1$: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address. Explanation: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps an IP address to a MAC address. When a host needs a MAC address for an IP, it sends a broadcast ARP request. The host with the matching IP responds with a unicast ARP reply containing its MAC address. So, Statement $\mathbf{1}$ is true. Statement $2$: A single TCP segment from a sender S to a receiver R cannot carry both data from S to R and acknowledgment for a segment from R to S. Explanation: A single TCP segment from S to R can carry both data and an acknowledgment (ACK) for a previously sent segment from R to S. This type of acknowledgment is known as a piggybacked ACK, where the ACK is included in the same segment that carries the data. So, Statement $\mathbf{2}$ is false. Answer: $\mathbf{(B)}$ benzene06 answered Feb 27, 2025 • edited Feb 27, 2025 by benzene06 benzene06 comment Sh

questions.explanation: According to the question,  A . GBN requires more bandwidth than SR ARQ is wrong. The implementation of GBN is very simple compared to the complex structure of SR ARQ. So it requires lesser load on link in terms of Bandwidth than selective repeat. A is False. B.  Error probability in GBN is more is True. Since there are repeated transmission of packets in the window even if they were transmitted before, it increases the probabilty as more packets are being sent in comparison to that of selective repeat where only the packets which got lost or ack not recievd were resent. B is True. C.  $Rwnd+Swnd <= ASN $ for Selective Repeat and for GBN $Windowsize +1 <= ASN$. this clearly shows that more sequence number is reuired for SR than that of GBN. So C is false. D.   Since GBN is light in terms of complexity, its CPU usage will definitely be less than that of SR. So D is True. E .    Go Back N uses Cumulative Acknowledgement and SR uses Individual Ack

questions.explanation: To calculate X−Y (the size of the last fragment minus the value of the More Fragments (MF) flag for the 4th fragment), let's go through the problem step by step. Step 1: Determine the IP Datagram Size and Fragmentation The IP datagram has a total size of 3200 bytes . The Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) for the link is 570 bytes . The header size is assumed to be the minimum, which is 20 bytes (the standard IPv4 header). Step 2: Determine the Payload Size The payload is the data portion of the datagram excluding the header:  $\text{Payload Size} = 3200 \, \text{bytes} - 20 \, \text{bytes} = 3180$ Now, we need to fragment this payload into pieces that can fit into the 570-byte MTU, keeping in mind that the 20-byte header must be included in each fragment. Step 3: Fragment Size Calculation Each fragment can carry a maximum of 570 bytes , and the header is 20 bytes, so the data portion of each fragment is: $\text{Data per Fragment} = 570 \, \text{bytes} - 20 \, \text{bytes} = 550 $ S

questions.explanation: Propagation delay = 0.5 sec Bandwidth (B) = 4 Mbps Frame Length (L) = 2 KB of data Transmission delay=Td=L/B=(2KB)/4Mbps=(2*1024*8)/4000000=0.004096sec RTT (2-way latency) = Td+2 * Propagation delay =0.004096+ 2 * 0.5 = 1.004096 sec For max utilization efficiency =1 then         N*Td=RTT         N=RTT/Td         N=1.004096/0.004096         N=245.14 Number of Sequence Bits: Number of Bits in Sequence number = ceil(logN) Number of Sequence Bits = ceil(log2(245.14)) Number of Sequence Bits = 8 Therefore, the maximum number of bits required for the sequence number field is 8 bits. mdhussain answered Dec 19, 2024 • edited Dec 19, 2024 by mdhussain mdhussain comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation: (1) To create multiple zones of trust   Explanation: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is a separate network segment isolated by firewalls that contains public-facing servers (like web, mail, or DNS servers). It allows you to separate internal trusted networks from the untrusted internet , creating multiple zones of trust . This way, even if a public server is compromised, attackers cannot directly access your internal network. Find the estimated round trip time & time out in Jacobson's Algorithm. A. 28 m sec, 58 m sec B. 26 m sec, 52 m sec C. 26 m sec, 58 m sec D. 26 m sec, 56 m sec
questions.questionHtml:
In TCP, the current Round trip time is 20 m sec and Acknowledgements come after 32 m sec. use a = 0.5 and initial deviation as 4. Find the estimated round trip time & time out in Jacobson's Algorithm.
A. 28 m sec, 58 m sec
B. 26 m sec, 52 m sec
C. 26 m sec, 58 m sec
D. 26 m sec, 56 m sec
questions.explanation: PRTT 1 = 20ms (Predicted RTT) ARTT 1 = 32ms  (Actual RTT) a = 0.5 PD 1 = 4ms  (Predicted Deviation) AD 1 (Actual Deviation) = |PRTT 1 - ARTT 1 | = |32-20| = 12ms PD 2 = a*PD 1 + (1-a)*AD 1 = 0.5*4 + 0.5*12 = 8ms PRTT 2 = a*PRTT 1 + (1-a)*ARTT 1 = 0.5*20 + 0.5*32 = 26ms Time Out Time = 4*PD 2 + PRTT 2 = 4*8 + 26 = 58ms So, Option (C) is correct.
